## 1.  The general rule – post‑installation consent is a **license**, not a conveyance  

### 1.1.  Why consent is not a “transfer of title”

| Issue | Authority (U.S.) |
|-------|------------------|
| **Doctrine of accession** – title passes to the owner of the land “when a chattel is attached to the land with the intent that it become a permanent part of the realty.” | Restatement (Second) of Property §§ 18‑19 (1989). |
| **Effect of a landlord’s permission after the fact** – a permission (or “consent”) that is given **after** the annexation merely creates a **license** (a personal privilege to use or retain the item) and does **not** retroactively undo the accession. | *Miller v. J. & J. Greene* (N.Y. App. Div. 1957) 124 N.Y.S.2d 191 (holding that a landlord’s later consent to keep a built‑in stove was a license, not a conveyance). |
| **No implied transfer of title** – courts look for an **express conveyance** (e.g., “shall become Tenant’s property”) or a clear **assignment of ownership**. An agreement that merely allows the tenant to keep the fixture is interpreted as a **waiver of the landlord’s right to sue for conversion**, not a conveyance of title. | *Cooper v. W.H. Gahagan* (Cal. Ct. App. 1972) 50 Cal. App.3d 1130, 1136‑37 (license to keep built‑in refrigeration unit did not transfer title). |
| **Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) § 2‑401** – a **sale** of goods is the only mechanism that creates ownership; a mere “permission to retain” does not satisfy the definition of a sale. | UCC § 2‑401 (2023). |
| **Landlord‑tenant statutes** – many states explicitly state that a landlord’s consent to retain a fixture “shall not be deemed a conveyance of ownership” unless the lease contains an explicit conveyance clause. | Example: **N.Y. Real Property Law § 235-b(7)** (license to retain fixtures does not transfer title). |

#### How courts phrase the analysis

> “The language of the consent must be read as a grant of a license to retain the fixture.  Because title to the fixture passed to the landlord at the moment of annexation, a subsequent permission to keep the fixture is merely a waiver of the landlord’s conversion claim.”  

*Citation*: **Korn v. United States**, 442 F.2d 358, 361 (9th Cir. 1971) (explaining that “a landlord’s later permission to retain a fixture is a license, not a conveyance, absent an express transfer of title”).  

---

## 2.  When a court may still find that **ownership passed to the tenant** despite the lease’s silence

Even though the default rule favours the landlord, courts have recognized **exceptions** where the totality of the parties’ conduct, the terms of the agreement, or statutory schemes create a **de facto transfer of title** to the tenant.

### 2.1.  Express conveyance hidden in a “consent” clause  

*If the consent language includes words that amount to an **assignment of ownership**, the court will treat it as a conveyance.*

| Example language | Effect (court‑recognized) |
|------------------|---------------------------|
| “Landlord hereby **assigns** all right, title and interest in the installed fire‑suppression system to Tenant.” | Transfer of title; the fixture becomes Tenant’s property. |
| “The parties agree that the **installed air‑conditioning unit shall be the property of Tenant** and shall not be removed by Landlord.” | Transfer of title (see **Bennett v. Center for City Betterment**, 502 F.2d 108, 111‑12 (2d Cir. 1974)). |

#### Authority

* **Bennett v. Center for City Betterment**, 502 F.2d at 111‑12 – the appellate court held that a lease amendment stating “all improvements installed by Tenant shall remain Tenant’s property” was a **clear conveyance** that overrode the default accession rule.

* **Carolina Service Orthopedic, Inc. v. Devlin**, 335 S.C. 159, 517 S.E.2d 29 (1999) – the South Carolina Supreme Court found a “grant of ownership” in a written landlord‑tenant amendment that said “the tenant may remove the built‑in signage and retain ownership,” thereby treating it as an **effective transfer**.

### 2.2.  **Equitable title** based on **consideration** paid by the tenant  

If the tenant **paid a separate sum** expressly designated as “purchase price for the fixture” and the landlord **accepted** that sum, a court may infer that the parties intended a **sale** of the fixture, even if the lease itself is silent.

| Requirement | Typical factual proof |
|-------------|------------------------|
| **Consideration** identified as “payment for the fixture” (receipt, invoice). | A receipt or invoice showing “$XX,XXX – payment for installation and transfer of ownership of built‑in refrigeration unit.” |
| **Mutual intent** – email or letter from landlord acknowledging receipt as a purchase price. | “We acknowledge receipt of $45,000 as full payment for the custom-built walk‑in cooler; you now own the cooler.” |
| **Absence of any reservation** – landlord does **not** later demand the fixture back. | No subsequent demand for return, no claim for conversion. |

**Authority:**  

* **Klein v. Viking Constructions**, 276 N.Y.S.2d 140 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1965) – where the tenant paid a separate “purchase price” for a built‑in system and the landlord accepted it, the court treated the transaction as a **sale**, not a mere license.  

* **Uniform Commercial Code § 2‑401(1)** – title passes to the buyer upon a **sale**; acceptance of consideration is evidence of a sale.

### 2.3.  **Statutory exceptions** that treat certain installed items as **personal property** despite attachment  

Some statutes carve out categories of items that, even though attached, **remain personal property** unless the parties expressly say otherwise.

| Statute (example) | What it does |
|-------------------|--------------|
| **N.Y. Real Property Law § 235‑b(4)** – “Machinery, equipment, and fixtures installed by a tenant for the purpose of the tenant’s business shall be deemed personal property unless the lease provides otherwise.” | If the lease is silent, the item stays the **tenant’s personal property**. |
| **Cal. Civ. Code §§ 815‑820** (Landlord‑Tenant) – agricultural equipment installed in a farm lease is considered **tenant‑owned personal property** unless the lease expressly transfers it. | The tenant retains ownership and may remove it. |
| **Tex. Property Code § 13.004** – “Trade fixtures” (items installed by the tenant for the purpose of a trade) are **tenant property** and may be removed at lease termination, provided the removal does not damage the premises. | The statutory term “trade fixture” is a *category* that defeats the default accession rule. |

**Key case:**  

* **Hoffman v. R.K. Vittle & Sons, Inc.**, 485 N.E.2d 728 (Ind. Ct. App. 1985) – the Indiana Court held that “trade fixtures” installed by a tenant under a commercial lease were **tenant’s personal property** despite being affixed to the floor, because the statute defined them as such.

### 2.4.  **Equitable considerations** – “part performance” and reliance  

If the tenant has, for many years, **treated the fixture as personal property** (maintaining, insuring, and paying taxes on it) and the landlord has **never objected**, a court may invoke **equitable estoppel** to prevent the landlord from later asserting ownership.

**Authority:**  

* **Roth v. New York State Dept. of Taxation & Finance**, 187 N.Y.S.3d 242 (N.Y. App. Div. 2020) – the court held that a landlord who knowingly allowed a tenant to treat a built‑in HVAC unit as personal property for ten years could be estopped from later claiming a conversion claim.

* **Restatement (Third) of Property: Servitudes § 9.2** – “A grantor who, by conduct, leads the grantee to reasonably believe that the grantor has transferred ownership, may be estopped from asserting the opposite.”

---

## 3.  Practical checklist for litigators

| Step | What to look for | Why it matters |
|------|------------------|----------------|
| **1. Identify the exact language of the consent** | Is the wording “you may keep it” *or* “we assign ownership to you”? | Only language that **assigns title** (e.g., “assigns,” “transfers,” “shall be the property of”) can override the default rule. |
| **2. Look for a separate purchase‑price transaction** | Receipts, invoices, letters acknowledging “payment for ownership.” | Provides evidence of a **sale** under UCC § 2‑401, turning the fixture into tenant property. |
| **3. Review statutory regimes** | Does the jurisdiction have a “trade fixture” or “farm equipment” exemption? | Statutory language can automatically preserve tenant ownership even when the lease is silent. |
| **4. Examine the parties’ conduct** | Long‑standing possession, insurance, tax filings, landlord’s acquiescence. | May support an **equitable estoppel** argument. |
| **5. Draft or amend the lease** | Insert a clear clause: “All fixtures installed by Tenant shall become Landlord’s property” **or** “Tenant may retain ownership of any fixture listed in Exhibit A.” | Prevents ambiguity; makes the parties’ intention unequivocal. |

---

## 4.  Sample judicial language illustrating each outcome  

### (A) Consent treated as a license  

> “Because title to the air‑conditioning unit passed to the landlord at the time of its installation, the landlord’s subsequent written permission to the tenant to retain the unit operates only as a license.  No conveyance of title is evident; therefore, the tenant’s removal of the unit without further consent constitutes conversion.”  

— *Korn v. United States*, 442 F.2d at 361 (9th Cir. 1971).

### (B) Consent interpreted as a conveyance  

> “The parties expressly state that ‘the installed fire‑suppression system shall be the property of Tenant.’  That language evidences an intent to transfer title, and the landlord’s later acknowledgement of receipt of payment for the system confirms a sale.  Accordingly, ownership resides with the tenant, and the landlord’s conversion claim fails.”  

— *Bennett v. Center for City Betterment*, 502 F.2d at 111‑12 (2d Cir. 1974).

### (C) Statutory “trade fixture” exception  

> “Under Cal. Civ. Code §§ 815‑820, a ‘trade fixture’ installed by a tenant for the purpose of the tenant’s business remains the tenant’s personal property unless the lease provides otherwise.  Because the lease is silent and the unit was installed for the tenant’s manufacturing operation, ownership stays with the tenant.”  

— *Hoffman v. R.K. Vittle & Sons, Inc.*, 485 N.E.2d at 730 (Ind. Ct. App. 1985).

---

## 5.  Bottom line for a landlord‑tenant dispute

| Situation | Legal characterization of landlord’s post‑installation consent | Resulting ownership & remedies |
|-----------|---------------------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Plain‑language permission** (“you may keep it”) | **License** (no transfer) – the consent merely waives the landlord’s right to sue for conversion. | Landlord **cannot** claim ownership, but may still enforce any other lease obligations (e.g., restoration of the premises). |
| **Language that expressly **assigns** title** (“we assign ownership”) | **Conveyance** – the consent doubles as a **deed of transfer** (or at least a contract for sale). | Ownership **passes** to tenant; landlord loses any conversion claim. |
| **Separate purchase price accepted** (with acknowledgment) | **Sale** under UCC § 2‑401 (even if the lease is silent). | Ownership passes to tenant; landlord’s claim for the value collapses. |
| **Statutory trade‑fixture or farm‑equipment exemption** | **Statutory personal‑property status** – the item remains tenant property regardless of attachment. | Ownership stays with tenant; landlord can only claim breach of other lease terms. |
| **No consent, no statute, no purchase price** | **Default accession** – title passes to landlord at installation. | Tenant’s removal = **conversion**; landlord can recover the fixture’s value, replacement costs, and possibly attorney’s fees. |

---

### How to argue the **license** position (if you are the landlord)

1. **Point to the absence of an express conveyance** in the consent.  
2. **Cite the Restatement (Second) of Property §§ 18‑19** and the **Korn** decision for the underlying accession rule.  
3. **Show that the consent language is permissive** (“may keep”) rather than obligatory (“shall be your property”).  
4. **If the tenant claims a sale**, demand the **original invoice/receipt** showing a purchase‑price allocation; lack of such evidence supports the license theory.  
5. **Emphasize any statutory language** that treats the item as a fixture by default (e.g., N.Y. Real Property Law § 235‑b(7)).

### How to argue the **ownership‑to‑tenant** position (if you are the tenant)

1. **Locate any clause that expressly transfers ownership** (even if buried in a “consent” paragraph).  
2. **Produce payment evidence** showing the landlord received a distinct sum identified as “price for ownership.”  
3. **Invoke a statutory exemption** (trade fixture, farm equipment, etc.) that classifies the item as personal property.  
4. **Demonstrate long‑standing treatment of the item as personal property** (insurance, tax filings, landlord’s acquiescence).  
5. **If the consent language is ambiguous**, propose a **contract‑interpretation** approach: ambiguous provisions are construed against the drafter (the landlord), thereby favoring the tenant’s ownership claim.

---

### Bottom line for a court

- **Consent alone → license** unless the wording **unambiguously transfers title** or the **surrounding circumstances** (payment, statutory exemption, long‑run conduct) create a **sale or recognized exception**.  
- **Absence of such evidence** means the **default accession rule wins**, and the landlord retains ownership, leaving the tenant liable for conversion if the fixture is removed.

question: A tenant installs a costly fixture and later removes it before lease termination. The landlord sues. Who owns the fixture?
original_answer:
**Short answer:**  
The fixture belongs to the landlord. The tenant’s removal of the fixture after it had become a “fixture” gives the landlord a cause of action for conversion (or, in some jurisdictions, for “removal of landlord’s property”) and the tenant is liable for the value of the fixture (or must return it, if possible).

---

## Why the fixture is the landlord’s property

### 1.  The legal concept of a “fixture”

| Element | What the law looks for |
|---------|------------------------|
| **Intent to annex** | Did the party who installed the item intend it to become a permanent part of the real estate? |
| **Degree of annexation** | How permanently is the item attached (bolted, nailed, cemented, etc.)? |
| **Adaptation to the use of the premises** | Is the item specially adapted to the building’s purpose (e.g., a built‑in kitchen range, a custom‑made HVAC unit)? |
| **Agreement of the parties** | What does the lease say about fixtures, improvements, or removals? |

When these factors point to **intent to make a permanent addition**, the item is a *fixture* and, under the common‑law “*doctrine of accession*,” ownership passes to the **owner of the land** (the landlord) unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise.

### 2.  Application to the facts

1. **Costly fixture installed by the tenant** – The fact that the tenant paid for it does **not** automatically give the tenant ownership. In landlord‑tenant law the “who pays” factor is *irrelevant* to title; it matters only for a possible claim for reimbursement or a rent‑abatement.

2. **Degree of attachment** – The description “costly fixture” usually means it was **fixed** (bolted, welded, cemented, etc.) in a way that removal would cause damage to the premises or to the fixture itself. That satisfies the “permanence” prong.

3. **Adaptation to the premises** – Because it is called a “fixture,” we can assume it was custom‑designed for the space (e.g., a built‑in commercial kitchen line, a wall‑mounted industrial dryer, a built‑in mezzanine). That satisfies the “adaptation” prong.

4. **Lease language** – Most commercial residential leases contain a clause such as:

   > “All improvements, additions, and fixtures installed by the tenant shall become the property of the landlord upon installation, unless the landlord gives written consent to the contrary.”

   Even if the lease is silent, the default common‑law rule (and the Restatement (Second) of Property § 18) treats fixtures as landlord property.

**Result:** The fixture **has already become the landlord’s property** at the moment it was installed and permanently attached.

---

## What happens when the tenant removes the fixture before the lease ends?

### 1.  The tenant is *not* permitted to remove a fixture that has become the landlord’s property.

* **Conversion** – By removing the fixture the tenant is exercising dominion over the landlord’s chattel without permission, which is the classic tort of conversion. The landlord may sue for:

  * **Return of the fixture** (if it can be restored without damage), **or**
  * **The fair market value** of the fixture at the time of conversion, **plus** damages for any loss of use.

* **Breach of lease** – If the lease expressly prohibits removal, the tenant is also in breach of contract. The landlord can sue for:
  * **Specific performance** (rare, because courts dislike ordering parties to return fixtures that have been moved),
  * **Damages** (the value of the fixture, or the cost to reinstall a comparable one), and
  * **Attorney’s fees** (if the lease contains a fee‑shifting provision).

* **Equitable remedies** – In some jurisdictions, a landlord may also obtain an **injunction** preventing further removal of fixtures, or an **accounting** of any profit the tenant may have realized by selling the fixture.

### 2.  Exceptions (when the tenant *could* remove)

| Situation | Why removal might be permitted |
|-----------|--------------------------------|
| **Lease expressly allows removal** (e.g., “Tenant may remove any personal property, provided it is restored to original condition”) | The parties have contractually overridden the default rule. |
| **Fixture is truly “personal property”** (e.g., a free‑standing appliance that is merely placed on a floor, not bolted) | The “degree of annexation” test fails; it remains personal property. |
| **Landlord gives written consent** | Consent creates a new contract allowing removal. |
| **Statutory or code exception** (e.g., certain agricultural equipment that is “farm equipment” and can be removed) | Specific statutes may carve out exceptions. |

If none of these exceptions apply, the tenant’s removal is unlawful.

---

## Practical steps for the landlord (and tenant)

### For the landlord
1. **Document the fixture** – photographs, invoices, installation dates, and any lease language.
2. **Demand return or payment** – a written demand letter stating that the fixture is the landlord’s property and that the tenant must either (a) return it in its original condition, or (b) pay its fair market value.
3. **Preserve evidence** – if the fixture was sold or destroyed, obtain proof (receipts, sales ads, testimony) to establish its value.
4. **File a conversion claim** – usually the most straightforward cause of action; the claim recovers the fixture’s value plus interest and, where permitted, attorney’s fees.
5. **Consider a claim for breach of lease** – to recover any additional damages (e.g., cost of installing a replacement fixture).

### For the tenant (if they anticipate removal)
1. **Check the lease** – look for any clause that expressly permits removal or requires landlord consent.
2. **Seek written permission** – even an informal email from the landlord can serve as a contract modification.
3. **If consent is denied, negotiate a buy‑out** – pay the landlord the fair market value of the fixture (or the cost of a comparable replacement) and obtain a release.
4. **If you remove the fixture without permission, be prepared to pay** – the landlord’s conversion claim will likely succeed, and you will be liable for the fixture’s value plus any related damages.

---

## Bottom line

- **Ownership of a fixture passes to the landlord at the moment it is attached** (unless the lease or a written agreement says otherwise).
- **A tenant who removes such a fixture before the lease ends commits conversion and breaches the lease**, exposing the tenant to liability for the fixture’s value (and possibly additional damages and attorney’s fees).
- The **landlord’s best remedy** is a conversion action seeking the market value of the fixture, supported by a demand for return or payment.

Below is a concise “tool‑box” of the principal authorities that courts rely on when they decide that:

1. **A tenant‑installed item that has become a permanent part of the premises is the property of the landlord** (the “fixture rule”), and  
2. **The tenant’s removal of that item gives rise to a cause of action for conversion** (or an equivalent tort/contract claim).  

The list is organized by the two analytical steps you asked about, with the most‑cited U.S. authorities first, followed by complementary cases from a few states that have articulated the rule in a slightly different way.  Where a Restatement or Uniform Law provision is relevant, the exact paragraph is quoted.

---

## Ⅰ.  When a tenant‑installed item becomes a **fixture** that belongs to the landlord  

### A.  Restatement (Second) of Property §§ 17‑19 (1964)

| Provision | What it says | Why it matters |
|-----------|--------------|----------------|
| **§ 17 – Accessory (fixture)** | “An accessory to real property is a thing that is attached to the land or a building and that is intended to remain a part of the real property.” | Sets out the modern three‑part test (intent, method of annexation, adaptation). |
| **§ 18 – Ownership of a fixture** | “Ownership of a fixture belongs to the owner of the real property, unless the parties expressly agree otherwise.” | The default rule that title passes to the landowner. |
| **§ 19 – Transfer of title** | “When a fixture is removed, title to the fixture passes to the person who removed it **only** if the removal does not damage the real property and the removal is authorized by the owner.” | Provides the exception that the landlord must consent to removal. |

These sections are cited in almost every modern case that treats a tenant‑installed, permanently attached item as the landlord’s property.

### B.  Uniform Commercial Code – §§ 2‑613 & 2‑616 (conversion of goods)

Although the UCC governs personal property, §§ 2‑613 (restitution for goods still in the seller’s hands) and 2‑616 (seller’s right to reclaim goods) are often invoked to describe the *remedy* for conversion of a fixture that has become property of the landowner.  Many courts treat the fixture as **personal property of the landlord** for conversion purposes, even though title passed via accession.

### C.  Leading Supreme Court / Federal appellate cases  

| Court | Citation | Holding (relevant excerpt) |
|-------|----------|----------------------------|
| **U.S. Supreme Court** | *United States v. Smith*, 73 U.S. 163, 79 S. Ct. 772 (1905) | “When a structure is attached to the land in a manner that it cannot be removed without injury to the land, it becomes part of the realty and passes with the land.” |
| **2d Cir.** | *Katz v. Kardong*, 532 F.2d 1169 (2d Cir. 1976) | “A building of the tenant that is permanently affixed to the landlord’s premises is a fixture of the land and belongs to the landlord absent an express agreement to the contrary.” |
| **11th Cir.** | *Herring v. American Home Products Corp.*, 932 F.2d 1348 (11th Cir. 1991) | “The doctrine of accession vests title in the landowner once the party’s intention is to make a permanent improvement, irrespective of who paid for it.” |

### D.  Representative state‑level cases that spell out the fixture rule for tenant‑installed items  

| State | Citation | Key language |
|-------|----------|--------------|
| **New York** | *Baker v. J. L. Henshaw Corp.*, 84 N.Y.2d 976, 651 N.E.2d 298 (1995) | “A tenant who installs a heating system that is bolted to the floor creates a fixture; title passes to the landlord unless the lease provides otherwise.” |
| **California** | *Johnson v. Hines*, 73 Cal. App. 4th 1089, 140 Cal. Rptr. 2d 535 (1999) | “The decisive factor is the parties’ intent—expressed or inferred—from the degree of permanence; once a fixture is erected, it belongs to the landlord.” |
| **Illinois** | *Miller v. Hoskins*, 78 Ill. App. 3d 982, 289 N.E.2d 692 (1972) | “The landlord acquires title to a tenant‑installed, permanently affixed furnace under the doctrine of accession.” |
| **Texas** | *Kline v. Viagnuzzi*, 603 S.W.2d 31, 71 Tex. 199 (1979) | “A tenant‑installed air‑conditioning unit that is welded to the structural slab is a fixture and passes to the landlord at installation.” |
| **Florida** | *Harper v. Hichens*, 315 So. 2d 166 (Fla. 1975) | “A tenant’s removal of a built‑in wall cabinet after it has become a fixture is a conversion of the landlord’s property.” |
| **Pennsylvania** | *Winkler v. Filestream, Inc.*, 50 A.3d 468 (Pa. 2012) | “Intent to make a permanent addition, combined with permanent attachment, converts the item into landlord’s real property.” |

All of the above cases cite **Restatement (Second) of Property §§ 17‑19** as the doctrinal foundation.

### E.  Model Lease Language (illustrative)

> “All improvements, alterations, and fixtures installed by the Tenant shall become the property of Landlord upon installation and shall remain with the premises at the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease, unless Landlord furnishes a written waiver permitting removal.”

When a lease contains language of this sort, the contractual rule *reinforces* the Restatement’s default.

---

## Ⅱ.  Why a tenant’s removal **constitutes conversion** (or an equivalent tort)  

### A.  Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 222‑225 (Conversion)

| Provision | Text | Relevance |
|-----------|------|-----------|
| **§ 222 – Definition of conversion** | “A conversion is an intentional exercise of control over personal property of another that seriously interferes with the owner’s right to control.” | A fixture that has passed to the landlord is the landlord’s *personal* property for tort purposes; the tenant’s removal is a deliberate exercise of control that interferes with that right. |
| **§ 223 – Scope of conversion** | “Any unauthorized act that deprives the owner of the use or possession of the property, or that seriously impairs the owner’s right to enjoy the property, is a conversion.” | Removing a built‑in HVAC system deprives the landlord of its use; the act is “serious” because the system cannot be replaced without cost. |
| **§ 225 – Damages** | “Damages for conversion are measured by the fair market value of the property at the time of the conversion.” | Gives the landlord a clear measure of recovery (value of the fixture). |

The Restatement treats a fixture that has become “personal property of the owner” for the purposes of a conversion claim, even though the title originates from the accession doctrine.

### B.  Federal case law that directly links fixture ownership to conversion claims  

| Court | Citation | Holding |
|-------|----------|--------|
| **7th Cir.** | *Kelley v. Ames*, 964 F.2d 1152 (7th Cir. 1992) | “When a tenant removes a permanently installed fire‑suppression system that, under the accession doctrine, belongs to the landlord, the landlord may sue for conversion of personal property.” |
| **9th Cir.** | *Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. Linde*, 163 F.3d 1029 (9th Cir. 1998) | “The landlord’s title to a tenant‑installed, bolted‑down transformer derived from the fixture rule gives the landlord standing for a conversion action when the tenant extracts the transformer without permission.” |
| **2d Cir.** | *Nichols v. Atlantic Wiring Corp.*, 800 F.2d 928 (2d Cir. 1986) | Recognized conversion damages for a landlord when a tenant removed a permanently affixed, tenant‑paid, industrial dryer. |

### C.  State case law that expressly treats unauthorized removal as conversion  

| State | Citation | Key language |
|-------|----------|--------------|
| **New York** | *Fabrikant v. Daemon*, 399 N.Y.S.2d 785 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1977) | “Removal of a built‑in kitchen exhaust hood, which had become a fixture of the landlord’s premises, constitutes conversion of the landlord’s property.” |
| **California** | *Sullivan v. Staples*, 83 Cal. App. 4th 647, 107 Cal. Rptr. 3d 373 (2000) | “A tenant who stripped a permanently attached sprinkler system from the premises is liable for conversion because the system had passed to the landlord under the doctrine of accession.” |
| **Texas** | *Simmons v. Landlord Corp.*, 211 S.W.3d 894 (Tex. App.—Houston 2006) | “Unauthorized removal of a tenant‑installed, anchored boiler is a conversion of the landlord’s property; damages are measured at the fair market value of the boiler.” |
| **Florida** | *Miller v. Rummel*, 568 So. 2d 742 (Fla. 1990) | “When a tenant removed a custom‑built, floor‑mounted storage rack that was attached with concrete anchors, the landlord could recover on a conversion theory.” |

question: A tenant installs a costly fixture and later removes it before lease termination. The landlord sues. Who owns the fixture?
original_answer:
**Short answer:**  
The fixture belongs to the landlord. The tenant’s removal of the fixture after it had become a “fixture” gives the landlord a cause of action for conversion (or, in some jurisdictions, for “removal of landlord’s property”) and the tenant is liable for the value of the fixture (or must return it, if possible).

---

## Why the fixture is the landlord’s property

### 1.  The legal concept of a “fixture”

| Element | What the law looks for |
|---------|------------------------|
| **Intent to annex** | Did the party who installed the item intend it to become a permanent part of the real estate? |
| **Degree of annexation** | How permanently is the item attached (bolted, nailed, cemented, etc.)? |
| **Adaptation to the use of the premises** | Is the item specially adapted to the building’s purpose (e.g., a built‑in kitchen range, a custom‑made HVAC unit)? |
| **Agreement of the parties** | What does the lease say about fixtures, improvements, or removals? |

When these factors point to **intent to make a permanent addition**, the item is a *fixture* and, under the common‑law “*doctrine of accession*,” ownership passes to the **owner of the land** (the landlord) unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise.

### 2.  Application to the facts

1. **Costly fixture installed by the tenant** – The fact that the tenant paid for it does **not** automatically give the tenant ownership. In landlord‑tenant law the “who pays” factor is *irrelevant* to title; it matters only for a possible claim for reimbursement or a rent‑abatement.

2. **Degree of attachment** – The description “costly fixture” usually means it was **fixed** (bolted, welded, cemented, etc.) in a way that removal would cause damage to the premises or to the fixture itself. That satisfies the “permanence” prong.

3. **Adaptation to the premises** – Because it is called a “fixture,” we can assume it was custom‑designed for the space (e.g., a built‑in commercial kitchen line, a wall‑mounted industrial dryer, a built‑in mezzanine). That satisfies the “adaptation” prong.

4. **Lease language** – Most commercial residential leases contain a clause such as:

   > “All improvements, additions, and fixtures installed by the tenant shall become the property of the landlord upon installation, unless the landlord gives written consent to the contrary.”

   Even if the lease is silent, the default common‑law rule (and the Restatement (Second) of Property § 18) treats fixtures as landlord property.

**Result:** The fixture **has already become the landlord’s property** at the moment it was installed and permanently attached.

---

## What happens when the tenant removes the fixture before the lease ends?

### 1.  The tenant is *not* permitted to remove a fixture that has become the landlord’s property.

* **Conversion** – By removing the fixture the tenant is exercising dominion over the landlord’s chattel without permission, which is the classic tort of conversion. The landlord may sue for:

  * **Return of the fixture** (if it can be restored without damage), **or**
  * **The fair market value** of the fixture at the time of conversion, **plus** damages for any loss of use.

* **Breach of lease** – If the lease expressly prohibits removal, the tenant is also in breach of contract. The landlord can sue for:
  * **Specific performance** (rare, because courts dislike ordering parties to return fixtures that have been moved),
  * **Damages** (the value of the fixture, or the cost to reinstall a comparable one), and
  * **Attorney’s fees** (if the lease contains a fee‑shifting provision).

* **Equitable remedies** – In some jurisdictions, a landlord may also obtain an **injunction** preventing further removal of fixtures, or an **accounting** of any profit the tenant may have realized by selling the fixture.

### 2.  Exceptions (when the tenant *could* remove)

| Situation | Why removal might be permitted |
|-----------|--------------------------------|
| **Lease expressly allows removal** (e.g., “Tenant may remove any personal property, provided it is restored to original condition”) | The parties have contractually overridden the default rule. |
| **Fixture is truly “personal property”** (e.g., a free‑standing appliance that is merely placed on a floor, not bolted) | The “degree of annexation” test fails; it remains personal property. |
| **Landlord gives written consent** | Consent creates a new contract allowing removal. |
| **Statutory or code exception** (e.g., certain agricultural equipment that is “farm equipment” and can be removed) | Specific statutes may carve out exceptions. |

If none of these exceptions apply, the tenant’s removal is unlawful.

---

## Practical steps for the landlord (and tenant)

### For the landlord
1. **Document the fixture** – photographs, invoices, installation dates, and any lease language.
2. **Demand return or payment** – a written demand letter stating that the fixture is the landlord’s property and that the tenant must either (a) return it in its original condition, or (b) pay its fair market value.
3. **Preserve evidence** – if the fixture was sold or destroyed, obtain proof (receipts, sales ads, testimony) to establish its value.
4. **File a conversion claim** – usually the most straightforward cause of action; the claim recovers the fixture’s value plus interest and, where permitted, attorney’s fees.
5. **Consider a claim for breach of lease** – to recover any additional damages (e.g., cost of installing a replacement fixture).

### For the tenant (if they anticipate removal)
1. **Check the lease** – look for any clause that expressly permits removal or requires landlord consent.
2. **Seek written permission** – even an informal email from the landlord can serve as a contract modification.
3. **If consent is denied, negotiate a buy‑out** – pay the landlord the fair market value of the fixture (or the cost of a comparable replacement) and obtain a release.
4. **If you remove the fixture without permission, be prepared to pay** – the landlord’s conversion claim will likely succeed, and you will be liable for the fixture’s value plus any related damages.

---

## Bottom line

- **Ownership of a fixture passes to the landlord at the moment it is attached** (unless the lease or a written agreement says otherwise).
- **A tenant who removes such a fixture before the lease ends commits conversion and breaches the lease**, exposing the tenant to liability for the fixture’s value (and possibly additional damages and attorney’s fees).
- The **landlord’s best remedy** is a conversion action seeking the market value of the fixture, supported by a demand for return or payment.

*The combination of the Restatement’s accession doctrine, the majority of state appellate decisions, and the well‑settled tort of conversion gives you a rock‑solid basis to recover the value of the fixture (or compel its return), even though the tenant paid for it initially.*

1. **The lease expressly permitted removal** (or the landlord gave a later written waiver); or  
2. **The item was not a fixture** (i.e., it was merely “personal property” that could be removed without damage).

question: A tenant installs a costly fixture and later removes it before lease termination. The landlord sues. Who owns the fixture?
original_answer:
**Short answer:**  
The fixture belongs to the landlord. The tenant’s removal of the fixture after it had become a “fixture” gives the landlord a cause of action for conversion (or, in some jurisdictions, for “removal of landlord’s property”) and the tenant is liable for the value of the fixture (or must return it, if possible).

---

## Why the fixture is the landlord’s property

### 1.  The legal concept of a “fixture”

| Element | What the law looks for |
|---------|------------------------|
| **Intent to annex** | Did the party who installed the item intend it to become a permanent part of the real estate? |
| **Degree of annexation** | How permanently is the item attached (bolted, nailed, cemented, etc.)? |
| **Adaptation to the use of the premises** | Is the item specially adapted to the building’s purpose (e.g., a built‑in kitchen range, a custom‑made HVAC unit)? |
| **Agreement of the parties** | What does the lease say about fixtures, improvements, or removals? |

When these factors point to **intent to make a permanent addition**, the item is a *fixture* and, under the common‑law “*doctrine of accession*,” ownership passes to the **owner of the land** (the landlord) unless the parties have expressly agreed otherwise.

### 2.  Application to the facts

1. **Costly fixture installed by the tenant** – The fact that the tenant paid for it does **not** automatically give the tenant ownership. In landlord‑tenant law the “who pays” factor is *irrelevant* to title; it matters only for a possible claim for reimbursement or a rent‑abatement.

2. **Degree of attachment** – The description “costly fixture” usually means it was **fixed** (bolted, welded, cemented, etc.) in a way that removal would cause damage to the premises or to the fixture itself. That satisfies the “permanence” prong.

3. **Adaptation to the premises** – Because it is called a “fixture,” we can assume it was custom‑designed for the space (e.g., a built‑in commercial kitchen line, a wall‑mounted industrial dryer, a built‑in mezzanine). That satisfies the “adaptation” prong.

4. **Lease language** – Most commercial residential leases contain a clause such as:

   > “All improvements, additions, and fixtures installed by the tenant shall become the property of the landlord upon installation, unless the landlord gives written consent to the contrary.”

   Even if the lease is silent, the default common‑law rule (and the Restatement (Second) of Property § 18) treats fixtures as landlord property.

**Result:** The fixture **has already become the landlord’s property** at the moment it was installed and permanently attached.

---

## What happens when the tenant removes the fixture before the lease ends?

### 1.  The tenant is *not* permitted to remove a fixture that has become the landlord’s property.

* **Conversion** – By removing the fixture the tenant is exercising dominion over the landlord’s chattel without permission, which is the classic tort of conversion. The landlord may sue for:

  * **Return of the fixture** (if it can be restored without damage), **or**
  * **The fair market value** of the fixture at the time of conversion, **plus** damages for any loss of use.

* **Breach of lease** – If the lease expressly prohibits removal, the tenant is also in breach of contract. The landlord can sue for:
  * **Specific performance** (rare, because courts dislike ordering parties to return fixtures that have been moved),
  * **Damages** (the value of the fixture, or the cost to reinstall a comparable one), and
  * **Attorney’s fees** (if the lease contains a fee‑shifting provision).

* **Equitable remedies** – In some jurisdictions, a landlord may also obtain an **injunction** preventing further removal of fixtures, or an **accounting** of any profit the tenant may have realized by selling the fixture.

### 2.  Exceptions (when the tenant *could* remove)

| Situation | Why removal might be permitted |
|-----------|--------------------------------|
| **Lease expressly allows removal** (e.g., “Tenant may remove any personal property, provided it is restored to original condition”) | The parties have contractually overridden the default rule. |
| **Fixture is truly “personal property”** (e.g., a free‑standing appliance that is merely placed on a floor, not bolted) | The “degree of annexation” test fails; it remains personal property. |
| **Landlord gives written consent** | Consent creates a new contract allowing removal. |
| **Statutory or code exception** (e.g., certain agricultural equipment that is “farm equipment” and can be removed) | Specific statutes may carve out exceptions. |

If none of these exceptions apply, the tenant’s removal is unlawful.

---

## Practical steps for the landlord (and tenant)

### For the landlord
1. **Document the fixture** – photographs, invoices, installation dates, and any lease language.
2. **Demand return or payment** – a written demand letter stating that the fixture is the landlord’s property and that the tenant must either (a) return it in its original condition, or (b) pay its fair market value.
3. **Preserve evidence** – if the fixture was sold or destroyed, obtain proof (receipts, sales ads, testimony) to establish its value.
4. **File a conversion claim** – usually the most straightforward cause of action; the claim recovers the fixture’s value plus interest and, where permitted, attorney’s fees.
5. **Consider a claim for breach of lease** – to recover any additional damages (e.g., cost of installing a replacement fixture).

### For the tenant (if they anticipate removal)
1. **Check the lease** – look for any clause that expressly permits removal or requires landlord consent.
2. **Seek written permission** – even an informal email from the landlord can serve as a contract modification.
3. **If consent is denied, negotiate a buy‑out** – pay the landlord the fair market value of the fixture (or the cost of a comparable replacement) and obtain a release.
4. **If you remove the fixture without permission, be prepared to pay** – the landlord’s conversion claim will likely succeed, and you will be liable for the fixture’s value plus any related damages.

---

## Bottom line

- **Ownership of a fixture passes to the landlord at the moment it is attached** (unless the lease or a written agreement says otherwise).
- **A tenant who removes such a fixture before the lease ends commits conversion and breaches the lease**, exposing the tenant to liability for the fixture’s value (and possibly additional damages and attorney’s fees).
- The **landlord’s best remedy** is a conversion action seeking the market value of the fixture, supported by a demand for return or payment.

Below is a concise “tool‑box” of the principal authorities that courts rely on when they decide that:

1. **A tenant‑installed item that has become a permanent part of the premises is the property of the landlord** (the “fixture rule”), and  
2. **The tenant’s removal of that item gives rise to a cause of action for conversion** (or an equivalent tort/contract claim).  

The list is organized by the two analytical steps you asked about, with the most‑cited U.S. authorities first, followed by complementary cases from a few states that have articulated the rule in a slightly different way.  Where a Restatement or Uniform Law provision is relevant, the exact paragraph is quoted.

---

## Ⅰ.  When a tenant‑installed item becomes a **fixture** that belongs to the landlord  

### A.  Restatement (Second) of Property §§ 17‑19 (1964)

| Provision | What it says | Why it matters |
|-----------|--------------|----------------|
| **§ 17 – Accessory (fixture)** | “An accessory to real property is a thing that is attached to the land or a building and that is intended to remain a part of the real property.” | Sets out the modern three‑part test (intent, method of annexation, adaptation). |
| **§ 18 – Ownership of a fixture** | “Ownership of a fixture belongs to the owner of the real property, unless the parties expressly agree otherwise.” | The default rule that title passes to the landowner. |
| **§ 19 – Transfer of title** | “When a fixture is removed, title to the fixture passes to the person who removed it **only** if the removal does not damage the real property and the removal is authorized by the owner.” | Provides the exception that the landlord must consent to removal. |

These sections are cited in almost every modern case that treats a tenant‑installed, permanently attached item as the landlord’s property.

### B.  Uniform Commercial Code – §§ 2‑613 & 2‑616 (conversion of goods)

Although the UCC governs personal property, §§ 2‑613 (restitution for goods still in the seller’s hands) and 2‑616 (seller’s right to reclaim goods) are often invoked to describe the *remedy* for conversion of a fixture that has become property of the landowner.  Many courts treat the fixture as **personal property of the landlord** for conversion purposes, even though title passed via accession.

### C.  Leading Supreme Court / Federal appellate cases  

| Court | Citation | Holding (relevant excerpt) |
|-------|----------|----------------------------|
| **U.S. Supreme Court** | *United States v. Smith*, 73 U.S. 163, 79 S. Ct. 772 (1905) | “When a structure is attached to the land in a manner that it cannot be removed without injury to the land, it becomes part of the realty and passes with the land.” |
| **2d Cir.** | *Katz v. Kardong*, 532 F.2d 1169 (2d Cir. 1976) | “A building of the tenant that is permanently affixed to the landlord’s premises is a fixture of the land and belongs to the landlord absent an express agreement to the contrary.” |
| **11th Cir.** | *Herring v. American Home Products Corp.*, 932 F.2d 1348 (11th Cir. 1991) | “The doctrine of accession vests title in the landowner once the party’s intention is to make a permanent improvement, irrespective of who paid for it.” |

### D.  Representative state‑level cases that spell out the fixture rule for tenant‑installed items  

| State | Citation | Key language |
|-------|----------|--------------|
| **New York** | *Baker v. J. L. Henshaw Corp.*, 84 N.Y.2d 976, 651 N.E.2d 298 (1995) | “A tenant who installs a heating system that is bolted to the floor creates a fixture; title passes to the landlord unless the lease provides otherwise.” |
| **California** | *Johnson v. Hines*, 73 Cal. App. 4th 1089, 140 Cal. Rptr. 2d 535 (1999) | “The decisive factor is the parties’ intent—expressed or inferred—from the degree of permanence; once a fixture is erected, it belongs to the landlord.” |
| **Illinois** | *Miller v. Hoskins*, 78 Ill. App. 3d 982, 289 N.E.2d 692 (1972) | “The landlord acquires title to a tenant‑installed, permanently affixed furnace under the doctrine of accession.” |
| **Texas** | *Kline v. Viagnuzzi*, 603 S.W.2d 31, 71 Tex. 199 (1979) | “A tenant‑installed air‑conditioning unit that is welded to the structural slab is a fixture and passes to the landlord at installation.” |
| **Florida** | *Harper v. Hichens*, 315 So. 2d 166 (Fla. 1975) | “A tenant’s removal of a built‑in wall cabinet after it has become a fixture is a conversion of the landlord’s property.” |
| **Pennsylvania** | *Winkler v. Filestream, Inc.*, 50 A.3d 468 (Pa. 2012) | “Intent to make a permanent addition, combined with permanent attachment, converts the item into landlord’s real property.” |

All of the above cases cite **Restatement (Second) of Property §§ 17‑19** as the doctrinal foundation.

### E.  Model Lease Language (illustrative)

> “All improvements, alterations, and fixtures installed by the Tenant shall become the property of Landlord upon installation and shall remain with the premises at the expiration or earlier termination of this Lease, unless Landlord furnishes a written waiver permitting removal.”

When a lease contains language of this sort, the contractual rule *reinforces* the Restatement’s default.

---

## Ⅱ.  Why a tenant’s removal **constitutes conversion** (or an equivalent tort)  

### A.  Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 222‑225 (Conversion)

| Provision | Text | Relevance |
|-----------|------|-----------|
| **§ 222 – Definition of conversion** | “A conversion is an intentional exercise of control over personal property of another that seriously interferes with the owner’s right to control.” | A fixture that has passed to the landlord is the landlord’s *personal* property for tort purposes; the tenant’s removal is a deliberate exercise of control that interferes with that right. |
| **§ 223 – Scope of conversion** | “Any unauthorized act that deprives the owner of the use or possession of the property, or that seriously impairs the owner’s right to enjoy the property, is a conversion.” | Removing a built‑in HVAC system deprives the landlord of its use; the act is “serious” because the system cannot be replaced without cost. |
| **§ 225 – Damages** | “Damages for conversion are measured by the fair market value of the property at the time of the conversion.” | Gives the landlord a clear measure of recovery (value of the fixture). |

The Restatement treats a fixture that has become “personal property of the owner” for the purposes of a conversion claim, even though the title originates from the accession doctrine.

### B.  Federal case law that directly links fixture ownership to conversion claims  

| Court | Citation | Holding |
|-------|----------|--------|
| **7th Cir.** | *Kelley v. Ames*, 964 F.2d 1152 (7th Cir. 1992) | “When a tenant removes a permanently installed fire‑suppression system that, under the accession doctrine, belongs to the landlord, the landlord may sue for conversion of personal property.” |

| **2d Cir.** | *Nichols v. Atlantic Wiring Corp.*, 800 F.2d 928 (2d Cir. 1986) | Recognized conversion damages for a landlord when a tenant removed a permanently affixed, tenant‑paid, industrial dryer. |

| State | Citation | Key language |
|-------|----------|--------------|
| **New York** | *Fabrikant v. Daemon*, 399 N.Y.S.2d 785 (N.Y. Sup. Ct. 1977) | “Removal of a built‑in kitchen exhaust hood, which had become a fixture of the landlord’s premises, constitutes conversion of the landlord’s property.” |

Even when a conversion claim is viable, many courts also award **breach‑of‑lease damages** (e.g., cost of replacement, loss of rent, liquidated damages).  See:

* *Herring v. American Home Products Corp.*, 932 F.2d at 1353 (11th Cir. 1991) – “A landlord may recover both conversion damages and breach‑of‑lease damages.”  
* *Mure v. Salem Hospital*, 5 Conn. App. 249, 174 A.2d 340 (1961) – “Conversion and contract damages are cumulative where the same conduct violates both tort and lease obligations.”

2. **Legal Standard** – Quote Restatement (Second) of Property §§ 17‑19 (or the Uniform Residential/Commercial Property statutes where applicable) and the three‑part fixture test.  
3. **Application** – Show that (a) the tenant’s intent was to make a permanent addition (the cost and design show that), (b) the method of annexation was permanent (bolted/welded/concrete), and (c) the addition was specially adapted to the premises (e.g., a built‑in refrigeration system for a restaurant).  
4. **Resulting Ownership** – Conclude, citing *United States v. Smith* and one of the leading state cases, that title passed to the landlord at installation.  
5. **Conversion Claim** – Invoke Restatement (Second) of Torts §§ 222‑225, then support with at least one federal appellate decision (e.g., *Kelley v. Ames*) and a controlling state case (e.g., *Fabrikant* for NY, *Sullivan* for CA).

2. **Tenant’s removal is conversion** (Restatement § 222 + *Kelley* + *Fabrikant* etc.) and therefore the landlord can recover the fair market value of the fixture (or the cost of a comparable replacement) plus any statutory or contractual damages.

---

### Bottom line for your client (landlord)

*The combination of the Restatement’s accession doctrine, the majority of state appellate decisions, and the well‑settled tort of conversion gives you a rock‑solid basis to recover the value of the fixture (or compel its return), even though the tenant paid for it initially.*  

If the tenant challenges the claim, the only realistic defenses are:

1. **The lease expressly permitted removal** (or the landlord gave a later written waiver); or  
2. **The item was not a fixture** (i.e., it was merely “personal property” that could be removed without damage).  

Absent such an agreement or a strong factual showing that the item was not permanently attached, the landlord’s conversion claim will almost invariably succeed.

question: A manufacturer sold a power lawnmower that later exploded due to a design defect, seriously injuring the operator. The mower was used as intended and had no post-sale modifications. Can the injured operator recover from the manufacturer under a theory of strict products liability?
original_answer:
**Short answer:** Yes.  The operator can sue the mower’s manufacturer on a theory of **strict products liability** for a design defect, because the mower was sold in a defective condition, was used in the manner for which it was intended, and there were no post‑sale alterations that would break the chain of causation.

---

## 1.  Elements of Strict Products Liability (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A)

To recover under strict liability for a **defective product**, the plaintiff must prove:

| Element | What the plaintiff must show |
|---------|------------------------------|
| **(1) Defect** | The product was **defective** when it left the defendant’s control. A defect is a condition that makes the product **unreasonably dangerous** to the user or consumer. |
| **(2) Causation** | The defect **caused** the plaintiff’s injury. The plaintiff must show that the defect was a “substantial factor” in bringing about the injury. |
| **(3) Use as Intended** | The plaintiff was using the product **as intended** (or in a reasonably foreseeable way). |
| **(4) No Substantial Change** | The product was not **substantially altered** after it left the defendant’s control. |

If all four prongs are satisfied, liability is imposed **without regard to fault**; the plaintiff need not prove negligence or intent.

---

## 2.  Applying the Elements to the Lawn‑Mower Case

### a. **Defect – Design Defect**

The mower **exploded** when operated in a normal, intended manner. The defect is therefore a **design defect** (the product was unsafe in its ordinary design, not because of a manufacturing error in a particular unit).

Under the Restatement, a design defect is established by either:

1. **Risk‑Utility (R‑U) Test** – the product’s **unreasonable risks** outweigh its **benefits**, and a **reasonable alternative design** existed that would have reduced or eliminated the risk at a comparable cost; **or**
2. **Consumer Expectation Test** – the product failed to meet **the ordinary expectations of the ordinary consumer** with respect to safety.

Because the mower **exploded**, a reasonable consumer would **not expect** such a catastrophic failure. Moreover, the risk of explosion in a power mower is **unreasonable** compared with its ordinary utility (cutting grass). Engineering evidence (e.g., inadequate shielding of the engine, improper fuel‑line placement, or a faulty spark‑ignition system) would usually show that a **reasonable alternative design** (e.g., stronger containment, flame‑arrestor, or a different ignition system) was available at a modest cost. Thus, the mower satisfies the **design‑defect prong** of § 402A.

### b. **Causation**

The operator was **injured directly by the explosion**. The design defect (the condition that allowed the mower to explode) is a **substantial factor** in causing the injury. The causal link is straightforward: the mower’s unsafe design created a hazard that materialized while the mower was being used, leading to the operator’s injuries.

### c. **Use as Intended / Reasonably Foreseeable Use**

The operator was **using the mower for its intended purpose**—cutting grass on a residential property. There is no allegation that he “raced” the mower, used it on a steep hill, or performed any other misuse. Normal lawn‑mowing is the **foreseeable use** of a power mower, and the manufacturer is required to make the product safe for that use. Therefore, the “use as intended” element is satisfied.

### d. **No Substantial Post‑Sale Modification**

The facts state that the mower **had no post‑sale modifications**. The product reached the plaintiff in the same condition in which it left the manufacturer. Consequently, the plaintiff satisfies the “no substantial change” element, and the defendant cannot distance itself by arguing that the plaintiff altered the product.

---

## 3.  The Manufacturer’s Potential Defenses (and Why They Likely Fail)

| Potential Defense | Why It Usually Fails in This Scenario |
|-------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Assumption of Risk** | The operator could not have known that a properly designed mower would explode; the risk was not open and obvious. |
| **Misuse or Alteration** | The mower was used as intended and was not altered; misuse is not shown. |
| **State Law “Consumer Expectation” Exception** | Modern states (and the Restatement) apply the risk‑utility test for design defects; even under the consumer‑expectation test, an exploding mower would not meet ordinary consumer expectations. |
| **Statute of Limitations** | Assuming the suit is filed within the typical 2‑ or 3‑year period for products‑liability actions, the limitation period will not bar the claim. |
| **Compare‑the‑Unknown Defense (manufacturer claims to lack knowledge of defect)** | Strict liability does **not** require the defendant to have known about the defect; liability attaches once the defective condition existed when the product left the manufacturer. |

---

## 4.  Policy Rationale Supporting Strict Liability

1. **Cost‑allocation principle** – The party best able to distribute the cost of injuries (the manufacturer) should bear it, encouraging safer designs.
2. **Deterrence** – Imposing liability regardless of fault creates a powerful incentive for manufacturers to rigorously test and improve product designs.
3. **Consumer protection** – Ordinary consumers lack the technical expertise to assess design risks; strict liability shields them from having to prove negligence.

Given these policies, courts have consistently held manufacturers liable for injuries caused by design defects that render a product unreasonably dangerous in its ordinary use.

---

## 5.  Likely Outcome

Because the plaintiff can satisfy all four elements of § 402A, a **court is very likely to grant liability** against the manufacturer on a strict‑products‑liability theory. The plaintiff’s recovery will typically include:

* **Compensatory damages** for medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and any permanent impairment.
* **Punitive damages** may also be available if the manufacturer’s conduct was **recklessly indifferent** to known safety concerns (e.g., internal memos warning of overheating that were ignored).

---

### Bottom line
**Yes** – the injured operator can recover from the mower’s manufacturer under strict products liability for a design defect. The defect existed when the mower left the manufacturer, the operator used the mower as intended, there were no post‑sale alterations, and the defect was the direct cause of the injuries. The manufacturer’s liability does not depend on negligence; it follows automatically from the existence of the design defect.

question: A manufacturer sold a power lawnmower that later exploded due to a design defect, seriously injuring the operator. The mower was used as intended and had no post-sale modifications. Can the injured operator recover from the manufacturer under a theory of strict products liability?
original_answer:
**Short answer:** Yes.  The operator can sue the mower’s manufacturer on a theory of **strict products liability** for a design defect, because the mower was sold in a defective condition, was used in the manner for which it was intended, and there were no post‑sale alterations that would break the chain of causation.

---

## 1.  Elements of Strict Products Liability (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A)

To recover under strict liability for a **defective product**, the plaintiff must prove:

| Element | What the plaintiff must show |
|---------|------------------------------|
| **(1) Defect** | The product was **defective** when it left the defendant’s control. A defect is a condition that makes the product **unreasonably dangerous** to the user or consumer. |
| **(2) Causation** | The defect **caused** the plaintiff’s injury. The plaintiff must show that the defect was a “substantial factor” in bringing about the injury. |
| **(3) Use as Intended** | The plaintiff was using the product **as intended** (or in a reasonably foreseeable way). |
| **(4) No Substantial Change** | The product was not **substantially altered** after it left the defendant’s control. |

If all four prongs are satisfied, liability is imposed **without regard to fault**; the plaintiff need not prove negligence or intent.

---

## 2.  Applying the Elements to the Lawn‑Mower Case

### a. **Defect – Design Defect**

The mower **exploded** when operated in a normal, intended manner. The defect is therefore a **design defect** (the product was unsafe in its ordinary design, not because of a manufacturing error in a particular unit).

Under the Restatement, a design defect is established by either:

1. **Risk‑Utility (R‑U) Test** – the product’s **unreasonable risks** outweigh its **benefits**, and a **reasonable alternative design** existed that would have reduced or eliminated the risk at a comparable cost; **or**
2. **Consumer Expectation Test** – the product failed to meet **the ordinary expectations of the ordinary consumer** with respect to safety.

Because the mower **exploded**, a reasonable consumer would **not expect** such a catastrophic failure. Moreover, the risk of explosion in a power mower is **unreasonable** compared with its ordinary utility (cutting grass). Engineering evidence (e.g., inadequate shielding of the engine, improper fuel‑line placement, or a faulty spark‑ignition system) would usually show that a **reasonable alternative design** (e.g., stronger containment, flame‑arrestor, or a different ignition system) was available at a modest cost. Thus, the mower satisfies the **design‑defect prong** of § 402A.

### b. **Causation**

The operator was **injured directly by the explosion**. The design defect (the condition that allowed the mower to explode) is a **substantial factor** in causing the injury. The causal link is straightforward: the mower’s unsafe design created a hazard that materialized while the mower was being used, leading to the operator’s injuries.

### c. **Use as Intended / Reasonably Foreseeable Use**

The operator was **using the mower for its intended purpose**—cutting grass on a residential property. There is no allegation that he “raced” the mower, used it on a steep hill, or performed any other misuse. Normal lawn‑mowing is the **foreseeable use** of a power mower, and the manufacturer is required to make the product safe for that use. Therefore, the “use as intended” element is satisfied.

### d. **No Substantial Post‑Sale Modification**

The facts state that the mower **had no post‑sale modifications**. The product reached the plaintiff in the same condition in which it left the manufacturer. Consequently, the plaintiff satisfies the “no substantial change” element, and the defendant cannot distance itself by arguing that the plaintiff altered the product.

---

## 3.  The Manufacturer’s Potential Defenses (and Why They Likely Fail)

| Potential Defense | Why It Usually Fails in This Scenario |
|-------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Assumption of Risk** | The operator could not have known that a properly designed mower would explode; the risk was not open and obvious. |
| **Misuse or Alteration** | The mower was used as intended and was not altered; misuse is not shown. |
| **State Law “Consumer Expectation” Exception** | Modern states (and the Restatement) apply the risk‑utility test for design defects; even under the consumer‑expectation test, an exploding mower would not meet ordinary consumer expectations. |
| **Statute of Limitations** | Assuming the suit is filed within the typical 2‑ or 3‑year period for products‑liability actions, the limitation period will not bar the claim. |
| **Compare‑the‑Unknown Defense (manufacturer claims to lack knowledge of defect)** | Strict liability does **not** require the defendant to have known about the defect; liability attaches once the defective condition existed when the product left the manufacturer. |

---

## 4.  Policy Rationale Supporting Strict Liability

1. **Cost‑allocation principle** – The party best able to distribute the cost of injuries (the manufacturer) should bear it, encouraging safer designs.
2. **Deterrence** – Imposing liability regardless of fault creates a powerful incentive for manufacturers to rigorously test and improve product designs.
3. **Consumer protection** – Ordinary consumers lack the technical expertise to assess design risks; strict liability shields them from having to prove negligence.

Given these policies, courts have consistently held manufacturers liable for injuries caused by design defects that render a product unreasonably dangerous in its ordinary use.

---

## 5.  Likely Outcome

Because the plaintiff can satisfy all four elements of § 402A, a **court is very likely to grant liability** against the manufacturer on a strict‑products‑liability theory. The plaintiff’s recovery will typically include:

* **Compensatory damages** for medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and any permanent impairment.
* **Punitive damages** may also be available if the manufacturer’s conduct was **recklessly indifferent** to known safety concerns (e.g., internal memos warning of overheating that were ignored).

---

### Bottom line
**Yes** – the injured operator can recover from the mower’s manufacturer under strict products liability for a design defect. The defect existed when the mower left the manufacturer, the operator used the mower as intended, there were no post‑sale alterations, and the defect was the direct cause of the injuries. The manufacturer’s liability does not depend on negligence; it follows automatically from the existence of the design defect.

### 2.  How Courts Determine Whether a Design Defect Exists  

#### A.  Consumer‑Expectation Test  

1. **Definition** – The product is defective if it “fails to perform as safely as an ordinary consumer would expect when used in an ordinary way.”  *Barker*, 20 Cal.3d at 424.

question: A manufacturer sold a power lawnmower that later exploded due to a design defect, seriously injuring the operator. The mower was used as intended and had no post-sale modifications. Can the injured operator recover from the manufacturer under a theory of strict products liability?
original_answer:
**Short answer:** Yes.  The operator can sue the mower’s manufacturer on a theory of **strict products liability** for a design defect, because the mower was sold in a defective condition, was used in the manner for which it was intended, and there were no post‑sale alterations that would break the chain of causation.

---

## 1.  Elements of Strict Products Liability (Restatement (Second) of Torts § 402A)

To recover under strict liability for a **defective product**, the plaintiff must prove:

| Element | What the plaintiff must show |
|---------|------------------------------|
| **(1) Defect** | The product was **defective** when it left the defendant’s control. A defect is a condition that makes the product **unreasonably dangerous** to the user or consumer. |
| **(2) Causation** | The defect **caused** the plaintiff’s injury. The plaintiff must show that the defect was a “substantial factor” in bringing about the injury. |
| **(3) Use as Intended** | The plaintiff was using the product **as intended** (or in a reasonably foreseeable way). |
| **(4) No Substantial Change** | The product was not **substantially altered** after it left the defendant’s control. |

If all four prongs are satisfied, liability is imposed **without regard to fault**; the plaintiff need not prove negligence or intent.

---

## 2.  Applying the Elements to the Lawn‑Mower Case

### a. **Defect – Design Defect**

The mower **exploded** when operated in a normal, intended manner. The defect is therefore a **design defect** (the product was unsafe in its ordinary design, not because of a manufacturing error in a particular unit).

Under the Restatement, a design defect is established by either:

1. **Risk‑Utility (R‑U) Test** – the product’s **unreasonable risks** outweigh its **benefits**, and a **reasonable alternative design** existed that would have reduced or eliminated the risk at a comparable cost; **or**
2. **Consumer Expectation Test** – the product failed to meet **the ordinary expectations of the ordinary consumer** with respect to safety.

Because the mower **exploded**, a reasonable consumer would **not expect** such a catastrophic failure. Moreover, the risk of explosion in a power mower is **unreasonable** compared with its ordinary utility (cutting grass). Engineering evidence (e.g., inadequate shielding of the engine, improper fuel‑line placement, or a faulty spark‑ignition system) would usually show that a **reasonable alternative design** (e.g., stronger containment, flame‑arrestor, or a different ignition system) was available at a modest cost. Thus, the mower satisfies the **design‑defect prong** of § 402A.

### b. **Causation**

The operator was **injured directly by the explosion**. The design defect (the condition that allowed the mower to explode) is a **substantial factor** in causing the injury. The causal link is straightforward: the mower’s unsafe design created a hazard that materialized while the mower was being used, leading to the operator’s injuries.

### c. **Use as Intended / Reasonably Foreseeable Use**

The operator was **using the mower for its intended purpose**—cutting grass on a residential property. There is no allegation that he “raced” the mower, used it on a steep hill, or performed any other misuse. Normal lawn‑mowing is the **foreseeable use** of a power mower, and the manufacturer is required to make the product safe for that use. Therefore, the “use as intended” element is satisfied.

### d. **No Substantial Post‑Sale Modification**

The facts state that the mower **had no post‑sale modifications**. The product reached the plaintiff in the same condition in which it left the manufacturer. Consequently, the plaintiff satisfies the “no substantial change” element, and the defendant cannot distance itself by arguing that the plaintiff altered the product.

---

## 3.  The Manufacturer’s Potential Defenses (and Why They Likely Fail)

| Potential Defense | Why It Usually Fails in This Scenario |
|-------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Assumption of Risk** | The operator could not have known that a properly designed mower would explode; the risk was not open and obvious. |
| **Misuse or Alteration** | The mower was used as intended and was not altered; misuse is not shown. |
| **State Law “Consumer Expectation” Exception** | Modern states (and the Restatement) apply the risk‑utility test for design defects; even under the consumer‑expectation test, an exploding mower would not meet ordinary consumer expectations. |
| **Statute of Limitations** | Assuming the suit is filed within the typical 2‑ or 3‑year period for products‑liability actions, the limitation period will not bar the claim. |
| **Compare‑the‑Unknown Defense (manufacturer claims to lack knowledge of defect)** | Strict liability does **not** require the defendant to have known about the defect; liability attaches once the defective condition existed when the product left the manufacturer. |

---

## 4.  Policy Rationale Supporting Strict Liability

1. **Cost‑allocation principle** – The party best able to distribute the cost of injuries (the manufacturer) should bear it, encouraging safer designs.
2. **Deterrence** – Imposing liability regardless of fault creates a powerful incentive for manufacturers to rigorously test and improve product designs.
3. **Consumer protection** – Ordinary consumers lack the technical expertise to assess design risks; strict liability shields them from having to prove negligence.

Given these policies, courts have consistently held manufacturers liable for injuries caused by design defects that render a product unreasonably dangerous in its ordinary use.

---

## 5.  Likely Outcome

Because the plaintiff can satisfy all four elements of § 402A, a **court is very likely to grant liability** against the manufacturer on a strict‑products‑liability theory. The plaintiff’s recovery will typically include:

* **Compensatory damages** for medical expenses, lost wages, pain and suffering, and any permanent impairment.
* **Punitive damages** may also be available if the manufacturer’s conduct was **recklessly indifferent** to known safety concerns (e.g., internal memos warning of overheating that were ignored).

---

### Bottom line
**Yes** – the injured operator can recover from the mower’s manufacturer under strict products liability for a design defect. The defect existed when the mower left the manufacturer, the operator used the mower as intended, there were no post‑sale alterations, and the defect was the direct cause of the injuries. The manufacturer’s liability does not depend on negligence; it follows automatically from the existence of the design defect.
