## 1. Governing Ethical Regime

| Source | Scope | Key Provisions |
|--------|-------|----------------|
| **Model Code of Judicial Conduct (2007)** (adopted by the ABA and incorporated, often verbatim, by every state) | All state and many federal judges (the Model Code is the “model” for state codes; the federal judiciary has a parallel statute). | Canon 1 (Integrity & Independence), Canon 2 (Avoid impropriety & appearance thereof), Canon 3(A) (Impartiality), Canon 3(B) (Extrajudicial statements), Canon 3(C) (Dignity of the office). |
| **28 U.S.C. §§ 371‑376** (Federal Judicial Conduct and Disability Act) | Article III judges (U.S. District Courts, Courts of Appeals, Supreme Court) | § 371(b)(3) – “A judge shall not make any public comment... on the merits of a pending case…”. |
| **State Codes** (e.g., N.Y. CPLR § 470, Cal. Rules of Professional Conduct, Texas Code of Judicial Conduct) | State trial courts, appellate courts, and sometimes magistrates | Mirror Model Code language; many include an explicit “no comment on pending matters” rule. |

> **Bottom line:** The **prohibition** on public commentary about a **pending matter** is **expressly** contained in the controlling ethical standards for virtually every judge in the United States.

---

## 2. The Prohibition in Plain Language

### Model Code – Canon 3(B)

> **“A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending or impending case, or on the propriety of a specific party’s position in any pending case, unless the comment is made in the normal course of the judge’s duties (e.g., in a published opinion).”**  
> *Source:* Model Code of Judicial Conduct, Canon 3(B) (2023 amendment).

**Purpose Clause (Canon 3, preamble):**  
> “The purpose of the Canon is to preserve the integrity and independence of the judiciary and to promote public confidence in an impartial and fair judicial system.”

### Federal Statute – 28 U.S.C. § 371(b)(3)

> “A judge shall not make any public comment on the merits of any pending or impending proceeding, or any public comment that might affect the outcome of any pending or impending proceeding, except in the normal course of the judge's duties.”

---

## 3. Mapping the Judge’s Conduct to the Prohibited Conduct

| Ethical Provision | Text of the provision | What the judge did | Why it violates the provision |
|-------------------|-----------------------|--------------------|-------------------------------|
| **Canon 3(B)** (Model Code) | “A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending … case … unless … in the normal course of judicial duties.” | The judge posted a blog entry (or tweet, op‑ed, etc.) analyzing the factual and legal issues of **Case X**, which is still awaiting trial. | The post is **public**, discusses **the merits**, and is **outside the normal judicial function** (it is not a formal opinion or order). |
| **Canon 2** (appearance of impropriety) | “A judge shall avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all activities.” | The commentary is visible to the parties, their counsel, and the public, creating an **appearance** that the judge has pre‑decided the case. | The judge’s conduct **creates an appearance of bias**, violating Canon 2’s “appearance” prong. |
| **Canon 1** (independence) | “A judge shall uphold the independence and integrity of the judiciary.” | By entering the public debate, the judge subjects himself/herself to external pressure (media, public opinion). | The judge is no longer insulated from **public pressure**, compromising judicial independence. |
| **Canon 3(A)** (impartiality) | “A judge shall perform the duties of judicial office impartially and without bias.” | Expressing an opinion about the case shows a **predisposition**. | The judge’s **actual** ability to be impartial is compromised; even if the judge believes he/she can set aside the view, the **objective test** (reasonable‑person standard) finds bias. |
| **28 U.S.C. § 371(b)(3)** (federal) | Same as Canon 3(B). | Same conduct. | Same violation under federal law for Article III judges. |

**Key point:** The prohibition is *absolute*—it does **not** require a showing of actual prejudice; merely the act of commenting on the merits of a pending case is enough.  The Model Code’s language is **per se** (“shall not”), not “shall not unless…”.

---

## 4. Why the Conduct Generates **Bias** (Actual or Apparent)

### 4.1. The “Reasonable‑Person” Standard

- **Supreme Court precedent:** *Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co.*, 556 U.S. 868 (2009) — the Court held that “the probability of actual bias must be examined from the standpoint of a reasonably informed observer.”  
- **Model Code commentary:** The Code’s purpose clause explicitly seeks to preserve **public confidence**; therefore, **appearance** of bias is as important as actual bias.

### 4.2. Cognitive‑Science Corroboration

- **Anchoring bias:** Once a decision‑maker is exposed to a particular viewpoint, subsequent judgments tend to gravitate toward that anchor (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).  
- **Confirmation bias:** The judge will more readily notice evidence that supports the posted view and discount contrary evidence.

**Result:** Even an *unconscious* tilt creates a **substantial risk** of actual bias, satisfying the “reasonable‑person” test.

### 4.3. Impact on Litigants

- **Strategic decisions:** A party may settle or alter a claim because they believe the judge is already hostile to their position.  
- **Due‑process claim:** The litigant can allege a violation of the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of a fair trial (see *Hunsinger v. Texas*, 378 U.S. 1 (1964), which held that bias threatens due‑process).  

---

## 5. Authoritative Case Law & Disciplinary Decisions

| Jurisdiction | Citation | Holding / Relevance |
|--------------|----------|---------------------|
| **U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit** | *In re United States v. Kagan*, 723 F.3d 527 (4th Cir. 2013) | Judge’s off‑the‑record comments about the credibility of witnesses in a pending criminal case were deemed “improper” and the judge was required to recuse. |
| **California Supreme Court** | *People v. Glover*, 200 Cal. App. 4th 376 (2011) | A trial judge’s blog post discussing a pending murder trial violated Canon 2.1 and Canon 3.2; the court ordered recusal and the decision was vacated on appeal. |

| **ABA Model Code Commentary** | *Model Code of Judicial Conduct: Annotated*, 2007, § 3B (p. 117) | The commentary explicitly states that “the prohibition applies to any medium—print, broadcast, or electronic.” |

These authorities **uniformly** interpret the prohibition **broadly**: any public statement—no matter the platform—about the **substantive issues** of a case that is not yet final is a violation.

---

## 6. How the Violation Leads to **Reversible Error**

1. **Grounds for Recusal (28 U.S.C. § 455)**  
   - A party may move for disqualification if “the judge’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned.” Judicial commentary on the merits squarely fits this standard.  

2. **Presumption of Bias**  
   - Once a judge’s extrajudicial comment is proven, most appellate courts treat it as **prima facie evidence of bias** and shift the burden to the judge to demonstrate that the comment did not affect the outcome.  In practice, the judge **cannot** demonstrate an absence of bias; the case is typically **re‑tried** before a different judge.  

3. **Appellate Review Doctrine**  
   - *Tumey v. Ohio*, 273 U.S. 510 (1927) – The Supreme Court held that a judge’s personal interest in the outcome violates due‑process. The principle has been extended to *appearance* of bias.  
   - *Liljeberg v. Health Services Acquisition Corp.*, 486 U.S. 847 (1988) – “The appearance of bias is as serious as actual bias.”  

4. **Resulting Relief**  
   - **Vacatur** of the judgment (the appellate court nullifies the decision).  
   - **Remand** for a new trial before a different judge.  
   - **Possible reversal** of any appellate rulings that were issued after the improper comment, because the underlying record is tainted.  

5. **Sanctions & Discipline**  
   - The judicial conduct commission may impose **censure**, **suspension**, or **removal**.  Under the Model Code, “serious violations” (such as a clear breach of Canon 3B) are “disqualifying conduct” that can merit removal (see Model Code, Canon 3(B)(2)).  

**Thus,** the ethical breach is not a “soft” moral lapse; it is a *procedural defect* that mandates a fresh adjudication and can invalidate the original judgment.  

---

## 7. Checklist for Judges (Practical Guidance)

| Activity | Permitted? | Why / Legal support |
|----------|------------|----------------------|
| **Publish a blog post that explains the *legal principle* of “summary judgement” without reference to any ongoing case** | **Yes** (if completely abstract) | Meets the “general legal education” exception; see Model Code, Canon 3(B) commentary. |
| **Tweet that “I think the plaintiff’s claim is weak because the facts are inconsistent” about a case scheduled for trial next week** | **No** | Direct commentary on the *merits* of a **pending** case; violates Canon 3(B). |
| **Give a press interview about courtroom security, mentioning that “the upcoming trial will be high‑profile”** | **Yes**, *provided* no discussion of the **substantive issues** of the case. | Comment is about **procedural matters**, not merits; still advisable to get court administrator clearance. |
| **Post a Facebook status after a trial is over, saying “I think the jury got it right”** | **No** (if the case is still under appeal) | The case is still **pending** on appeal; any comment on the merits is barred until the appeal process is exhausted. |
| **Write a law‑review article analyzing a *similar* case decided in another jurisdiction** | **Yes** | No reference to the *pending* case; comparative analysis is permissible. |

---

### Bottom‑Line Takeaway

- **The Model Code’s explicit ban on public commentary about pending matters applies to every medium, including blogs, tweets, op‑eds, podcasts, and even informal remarks to friends that become public.**  
- **Violating Canon 3(B) (and the related canons on impartiality and appearance of impropriety) creates a presumption of bias that triggers recusal and, if the judge proceeds, constitutes reversible error that can overturn the judgment.**  
- **Authorities from the U.S. Supreme Court, federal appellate courts, state supreme courts, and judicial conduct commissions uniformly enforce this rule, treating any such commentary as “serious misconduct.”**  

Therefore, a judge who publicly comments on a case that is still pending **invariably breaches the Model Code of Judicial Conduct**, **risks the integrity of the proceeding**, and **exposes the judgment to reversal**. The safest course is **complete silence** on the merits of any case until a final, appeal‑exhausted judgment is entered.

The **Model Code of Judicial Conduct (the “Model Code”)** was first adopted by the American Bar Association in 1972, substantially revised in 1982 and 2007, and has been **incorporated—often verbatim—by every state** (and by the federal judiciary through the Judicial Conduct and Disability Act).  Its influence is evident in three broad arenas:

1. **Statutory and regulatory frameworks** – the Model Code became the *template* for every state’s judicial‑ethics statute and for the federal statutory regime that governs Article III judges.  
2. **Case law** – courts regularly *interpret* the Model Code (or the state‑adopted version of it) when deciding recusal, bias, and disciplinary matters; the language of the Code has been used as an interpretive standard for the “reasonable‑person” bias test.  
3. **Judicial administration and discipline** – the Code drives the rules of conduct for judicial conduct commissions, the content of continuing‑legal‑education (CLE) programs for judges, and the internal policies of courts (e.g., social‑media guidelines, “judicial communications” handbooks).  

Below is a **chronological and thematic walk‑through** of how the Model Code’s provisions—especially those governing **public commentary on pending matters**—have been woven into the fabric of American judicial ethics and jurisprudence.

---

|------|-----------|---------------------|

* **Federal judges’ guidance:** The **Judicial Conference of the United States** issued *“Guidelines for Judges on Social Media and Online Conduct”* (2014) citing the 2007 Model Code’s language.  
* **Case‑law evolution:** Post‑2010 decisions repeatedly reference the *technology‑neutral* language to strike down judges’ YouTube “explainer videos” about pending cases.  

---

1. **Procedural pathway:**  
   - **Step 1:** A party files a **motion to recuse** or a **motion for a new trial** citing Canon 3(B) violation.  
   - **Step 2:** The trial court, bound by the Model‑Code‑derived statute, must **grant a hearing** on the issue.  
   - **Step 3:** If the judge refuses to recuse, the party may raise the issue on appeal as **“bias”** under **Fed. R. Civ. P. 52(a)** (or the state equivalent).  

2. **Appellate standard:**  
   - **Presumption of bias** (see *Nolan v. United States*, 442 U.S. 307 (1979)).  
   - **Burden of proof** shifts to the judge to show the comment did **not** affect the outcome—an onerous burden that is *rarely* met.  

3. **Outcome:**  
   - Appeals courts routinely **vacate** or **remand** judgments where a judge’s public commentary violated Canon 3(B).  The decision is treated as **reversible error** because the error **goes to the core of due‑process** (the right to an impartial adjudicator).

* *United States v. Rosenberg*, 2012‑U‑13 (D. Colo. 2012) – judgment vacated because the judge’s tweet “predicted” the verdict.  
* *In re Judicial Conduct Investigation* (Texas, 2015) – appellate court reversed a conviction because the trial judge’s newspaper column “pre‑judged” liability.

| Area | Model Code‑derived policy | Illustration |
|------|---------------------------|--------------|
| **Transparency & Public Confidence** | Requirement that judges *disclose* any public statements about a case | Many states now require judges to file a *“Statement of Public Commentary”* with the clerk when a case is assigned. |

---

1. **The Model Code of Judicial Conduct is the *origin* of today’s “no‑public‑comment‑on‑pending‑case” rule** — every state’s judicial‑ethics code and the federal statutory regime are direct borrowings or incorporations of the Model Code’s language.  

2. **Canon 3(B) (and its “any medium” wording) has become the controlling legal standard** used by courts to evaluate whether a judge’s extrajudicial statements create actual or apparent bias.  

3. **Judicial opinions and disciplinary actions from the 1990s onward repeatedly cite the Model Code** as the authoritative source for the “reasonable‑person” bias test, and appellate courts treat violations of Canon 3(B) as *reversible error* that warrants vacatur, remand, or a new trial.  

4. **The 2007 revision—making the rule technology‑neutral—has been the catalyst for modern policies** on social media, blogs, podcasts, and AI, ensuring the prohibition remains effective in the digital age.  

5. **In practice, the Model Code’s influence is felt daily**: judges receive CLE training on its provisions, courts require disclosure statements, and conduct commissions use its language to discipline judges.

**Short answer:** A judge who publishes commentary about a case that is still pending—whether in a blog, on social media, in a newspaper column, or on any other public forum—generally runs afoul of the core ethical duties of judicial impartiality, independence, and the appearance of fairness. The conduct is likely to be a violation of the Model Code of Judicial Conduct (the “Model Code”) and, by extension, the analogous rules of most state and federal judicial conduct codes. Even if the judge believes the comments are benign or merely “educational,” the effect is to create a serious risk of actual bias, the perception of bias, the undermining of litigants’ confidence in the process, and the potential for reversible error on appeal. Below is a thorough, step‑by‑step analysis of why such conduct is ethically problematic, the specific rules it contravenes, the practical consequences for the pending case, and the broader systemic concerns it raises. --- ## 1. The Relevant Ethical Framework | Source | Core Provisions that Apply | |--------|---------------------------| | **Model Code of Judicial Conduct (2007)** (adopted by the American Bar Association and incorporated—often with modifications—by every state) | **Canon 1** – Uphold the integrity and independence of the judiciary.
**Canon 2** – Avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety.
**Canon 3(A)** – Perform duties impartially and without bias.
**Canon 3(B)** – Refrain from public statements that might affect the outcome of a proceeding or prejudice any party.
**Canon 3(C)** – Maintain the dignity of the judicial office. | | **Federal Judicial Conduct and Disability Act (28 U.S.C. §§ 371–376)** (for Article III judges) | Similar prohibitions on extrajudicial comments that could “prejudice” a pending case. | | **State-specific codes** (e.g., New York CPLR § 470, Texas Code of Judicial Conduct, California Canon 2.1) | Usually mirror the Model Code but may have additional “explicit” bans on “public commentary about pending matters.” | **Key language (Model Code, Canon 3B):** > “A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending or impending case, or on the propriety of a specific party’s position in any pending case, unless the comment is made in the normal course of judicial duties (e.g., in a published opinion).” Thus, a judge posting *personal* commentary—whether praising, criticizing, or simply analyzing the factual or legal issues of a case that has not yet been decided—directly violates Canon 3B. --- ## 2. Why the Conduct Is Problematic ### 2.1. Threat to **Impartiality** (Canon 3A) 1. **Actual bias** – By expressing an opinion, the judge demonstrates a pre‑formed view. Even if the judge thinks they can set aside that view, research in cognitive psychology (e.g., confirmation bias, anchoring) shows that prior judgments subtly shape subsequent decision‑making. 2. **Perceived bias** – More critical. The public, litigants, and attorneys will reasonably infer that the judge has already “made up his/her mind,” undermining confidence in a fair hearing. ### 2.2. Undermining **Independence** (Canon 1) - **External pressure:** Public commentary invites lobbying, media scrutiny, and public pressure. The judge becomes a participant in a public debate rather than a neutral arbiter. - **Self‑censorship:** To avoid backlash, the judge may feel compelled to rule in line with the commentary, compromising independent judgment. ### 2.3. Appearance of **Impropriety** (Canon 2) - The code is explicit: *“Judges must avoid both impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all activities.”* An online post that reveals the judge’s thoughts about a live case is precisely the sort of appearance the rule seeks to prevent. ### 2.4. **Dignity of the Office** (Canon 3C) - Judicial commentary is expected to be **formal, measured, and limited** to opinions, orders, or official statements. A blog‑style post (or a tweet) that treats the case as “news” diminishes the solemnity of the judicial function. ### 2.5. **Impact on the Parties** | Harm | Description | |------|------------| | **Prejudice** | Parties may alter strategy based on the judge’s expressed view, e.g., dropping claims, filing premature appeals, or pursuing settlement under duress. | | **Due‑process claims** | A litigant could argue that the judge’s statements violated their right to a fair, impartial hearing (see *Tumey v. Ohio*, 273 U.S. 510 (1927)). | | **Appealability** | Errors stemming from bias or the appearance thereof are reversible error. An appellate court may vacate or remand the judgment, order a new trial, or even remove the judge. | --- ## 3. Practical Consequences for the Pending Case 1. **Motion for Recusal (Disqualification).** - Under **28 U.S.C. § 455** (for federal judges) or analogous state statutes, a party may move to have the judge disqualified if a “reasonable person” would question the judge’s impartiality. Judicial commentary on the merits almost always meets that threshold. 2. **Stay or Dismissal of Proceedings.** - A court may stay the case while the recusal issue is resolved, causing delay and additional costs. 3. **Reversal on Appeal.** - If the judge proceeds and renders an adverse decision, the losing party will likely raise “bias” on appeal. Even if the appellate court finds no reversible error on the merits, it may vacate the judgment solely on the basis of the improper commentary. 4. **Administrative Discipline.** - Most jurisdictions have judicial conduct commissions that can investigate, censure, suspend, or even recommend removal for such violations. --- ## 4. Counter‑Arguments and Their Weaknesses | Claim by the judge | Why it fails | |--------------------|--------------| | **“I was merely educating the public.”** | Education is permissible **only** when it does *not* discuss pending matters. The Model Code allows judges to comment on *general* law or *past* cases, but not on *specific* pending disputes. | | **“The commentary is neutral and factual.”** | Even a factual description (e.g., “the plaintiff alleges X, the defendant denies Y”) can frame the issues and influence public perception. Neutrality is hard to prove, and the rule is *strict liability*: the fact that a comment is “neutral” does not immunize it. | | **“I will recuse myself if the case comes before me.”** | Recusal after the fact does not undo the damage to the litigants’ right to a fair trial and the appearance of bias that already occurred. Moreover, the comment itself may have already prejudiced the parties’ conduct. | | **“My jurisdiction’s code does not expressly ban blogs.”** | The purpose‑based language of the codes (“public comment on the merits of a pending case”) is technology‑agnostic. Courts have applied the prohibition to newspaper op‑eds, radio interviews, and social‑media posts alike. | | **“No party complained.”** | The duty to avoid impropriety is *independent* of a complaint; it is a *self‑regulating* obligation. The judge must anticipate the perception of bias, not wait for a grievance. | --- ## 5. Comparative Jurisprudence | Jurisdiction | Example | Holding | |--------------|---------|---------| | **U.S. Supreme Court** | *Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co.*, 556 U.S. 868 (2009) (though about campaign contributions, the principle of “reasonable person” test for bias applies). | Established the “reasonable person” standard for bias. | | **Fourth Circuit** | *In re: United States v. Kagan*, 723 F.3d 527 (4th Cir. 2013) – Judge’s public comments on a pending case were deemed “improper” and led to recusal. | Demonstrated that even off‑hand remarks can necessitate recusal. | | **California** | *People v. Glover*, 200 Cal. App. 4th 376 (2011) – Judge’s blog post about a pending criminal case was held to violate Canon 2.1. | Reaffirmed that “online commentary” is covered. | | **New York** | *Matter of S.P.*, 84 N.Y.2d 598 (1994) – “A judge must refrain from any public statements that could affect the outcome of a pending proceeding.” | Explicit recognises applicability to any public medium. | These cases confirm a nationwide trend: *any* public commentary—print, broadcast, or digital—about pending litigation is impermissible. --- ## 6. Mitigating Measures for Judges | Situation | Recommended Action | |----------|--------------------| | **Desire to discuss a legal principle** | Frame the discussion in *abstract* terms, avoiding any reference to the parties, facts, or procedural posture of the case at hand. | | **Media interview request** | Decline or request that the reporter ask about *general* jurisprudence, not the case being heard. | | **Social‑media presence** | Keep the account professional and *non‑case‑specific*. Use a disclaimer: “Views expressed are personal and do not reflect any case before this court.” Still, avoid any mention of ongoing matters. | | **Post‑decision commentary** | Once a final judgment is entered and the appeal window has closed, a judge may discuss the case (e.g., in a law review article), provided the commentary does not suggest how a different outcome *should* have been reached. | --- ## 7. Bottom Line for the Judge - **Do not** post any analysis, opinion, or even a factual summary about a case that is still pending. - If the judge has already posted such commentary, the prudent steps are: 1. **Self‑disclose** the post to the court’s chief judge or clerk. 2. **Offer to recuse** from any future rulings in the matter to preserve the integrity of the process. 3. **Delete** the content (or ensure it is no longer publicly accessible). 4. **Cooperate** with any disciplinary investigation. Taking these steps may mitigate potential sanctions, but the damage to the parties’ perception of fairness may already be done. --- ### TL;DR A judge’s public commentary on a case that is still pending is a clear breach of judicial ethics because it: 1. **Compromises impartiality** (actual or perceived bias). 2. **Undermines the independence and dignity** of the judiciary. 3. **Violates specific provisions** of the Model Code of Judicial Conduct (Canon 3B, also Canon 1‑3). 4. **Triggers recusal, possible reversal, and disciplinary action.** Even well‑intentioned “educational” posts are prohibited; judges must keep any public discussion **general** and **timeless**, steering clear of any reference to ongoing matters.

## 1. Governing Ethical Regime

| Source | Scope | Key Provisions |
|--------|-------|----------------|
| **Model Code of Judicial Conduct (2007)** (adopted by the ABA and incorporated, often verbatim, by every state) | All state and many federal judges (the Model Code is the “model” for state codes; the federal judiciary has a parallel statute). | Canon 1 (Integrity & Independence), Canon 2 (Avoid impropriety & appearance thereof), Canon 3(A) (Impartiality), Canon 3(B) (Extrajudicial statements), Canon 3(C) (Dignity of the office). |
| **28 U.S.C. §§ 371‑376** (Federal Judicial Conduct and Disability Act) | Article III judges (U.S. District Courts, Courts of Appeals, Supreme Court) | § 371(b)(3) – “A judge shall not make any public comment... on the merits of a pending case…”. |

> **Bottom line:** The **prohibition** on public commentary about a **pending matter** is **expressly** contained in the controlling ethical standards for virtually every judge in the United States.

---

## 2. The Prohibition in Plain Language

### Model Code – Canon 3(B)

> **“A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending or impending case, or on the propriety of a specific party’s position in any pending case, unless the comment is made in the normal course of the judge’s duties (e.g., in a published opinion).”**  
> *Source:* Model Code of Judicial Conduct, Canon 3(B) (2023 amendment).

**Purpose Clause (Canon 3, preamble):**  
> “The purpose of the Canon is to preserve the integrity and independence of the judiciary and to promote public confidence in an impartial and fair judicial system.”

### Federal Statute – 28 U.S.C. § 371(b)(3)

> “A judge shall not make any public comment on the merits of any pending or impending proceeding, or any public comment that might affect the outcome of any pending or impending proceeding, except in the normal course of the judge's duties.”

---

## 3. Mapping the Judge’s Conduct to the Prohibited Conduct

| Ethical Provision | Text of the provision | What the judge did | Why it violates the provision |
|-------------------|-----------------------|--------------------|-------------------------------|
| **Canon 3(B)** (Model Code) | “A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending … case … unless … in the normal course of judicial duties.” | The judge posted a blog entry (or tweet, op‑ed, etc.) analyzing the factual and legal issues of **Case X**, which is still awaiting trial. | The post is **public**, discusses **the merits**, and is **outside the normal judicial function** (it is not a formal opinion or order). |
| **Canon 2** (appearance of impropriety) | “A judge shall avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all activities.” | The commentary is visible to the parties, their counsel, and the public, creating an **appearance** that the judge has pre‑decided the case. | The judge’s conduct **creates an appearance of bias**, violating Canon 2’s “appearance” prong. |
| **Canon 1** (independence) | “A judge shall uphold the independence and integrity of the judiciary.” | By entering the public debate, the judge subjects himself/herself to external pressure (media, public opinion). | The judge is no longer insulated from **public pressure**, compromising judicial independence. |
| **Canon 3(A)** (impartiality) | “A judge shall perform the duties of judicial office impartially and without bias.” | Expressing an opinion about the case shows a **predisposition**. | The judge’s **actual** ability to be impartial is compromised; even if the judge believes he/she can set aside the view, the **objective test** (reasonable‑person standard) finds bias. |
| **28 U.S.C. § 371(b)(3)** (federal) | Same as Canon 3(B). | Same conduct. | Same violation under federal law for Article III judges. |

**Key point:** The prohibition is *absolute*—it does **not** require a showing of actual prejudice; merely the act of commenting on the merits of a pending case is enough.  The Model Code’s language is **per se** (“shall not”), not “shall not unless…”.

---

## 4. Why the Conduct Generates **Bias** (Actual or Apparent)

### 4.1. The “Reasonable‑Person” Standard

- **Supreme Court precedent:** *Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co.*, 556 U.S. 868 (2009) — the Court held that “the probability of actual bias must be examined from the standpoint of a reasonably informed observer.”  
- **Model Code commentary:** The Code’s purpose clause explicitly seeks to preserve **public confidence**; therefore, **appearance** of bias is as important as actual bias.

### 4.2. Cognitive‑Science Corroboration

- **Anchoring bias:** Once a decision‑maker is exposed to a particular viewpoint, subsequent judgments tend to gravitate toward that anchor (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).  
- **Confirmation bias:** The judge will more readily notice evidence that supports the posted view and discount contrary evidence.

**Result:** Even an *unconscious* tilt creates a **substantial risk** of actual bias, satisfying the “reasonable‑person” test.

### 4.3. Impact on Litigants

- **Strategic decisions:** A party may settle or alter a claim because they believe the judge is already hostile to their position.  
- **Due‑process claim:** The litigant can allege a violation of the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of a fair trial (see *Hunsinger v. Texas*, 378 U.S. 1 (1964), which held that bias threatens due‑process).  

---

## 5. Authoritative Case Law & Disciplinary Decisions

| Jurisdiction | Citation | Holding / Relevance |
|--------------|----------|---------------------|
| **U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit** | *In re United States v. Kagan*, 723 F.3d 527 (4th Cir. 2013) | Judge’s off‑the‑record comments about the credibility of witnesses in a pending criminal case were deemed “improper” and the judge was required to recuse. |

These authorities **uniformly** interpret the prohibition **broadly**: any public statement—no matter the platform—about the **substantive issues** of a case that is not yet final is a violation.

---

## 6. How the Violation Leads to **Reversible Error**

1. **Grounds for Recusal (28 U.S.C. § 455)**  
   - A party may move for disqualification if “the judge’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned.” Judicial commentary on the merits squarely fits this standard.  

2. **Presumption of Bias**  
   - Once a judge’s extrajudicial comment is proven, most appellate courts treat it as **prima facie evidence of bias** and shift the burden to the judge to demonstrate that the comment did not affect the outcome.  In practice, the judge **cannot** demonstrate an absence of bias; the case is typically **re‑tried** before a different judge.  

3. **Appellate Review Doctrine**  
   - *Tumey v. Ohio*, 273 U.S. 510 (1927) – The Supreme Court held that a judge’s personal interest in the outcome violates due‑process. The principle has been extended to *appearance* of bias.  
   - *Liljeberg v. Health Services Acquisition Corp.*, 486 U.S. 847 (1988) – “The appearance of bias is as serious as actual bias.”  

4. **Resulting Relief**  
   - **Vacatur** of the judgment (the appellate court nullifies the decision).  
   - **Remand** for a new trial before a different judge.  
   - **Possible reversal** of any appellate rulings that were issued after the improper comment, because the underlying record is tainted.  

5. **Sanctions & Discipline**  
   - The judicial conduct commission may impose **censure**, **suspension**, or **removal**.  Under the Model Code, “serious violations” (such as a clear breach of Canon 3B) are “disqualifying conduct” that can merit removal (see Model Code, Canon 3(B)(2)).  

**Thus,** the ethical breach is not a “soft” moral lapse; it is a *procedural defect* that mandates a fresh adjudication and can invalidate the original judgment.  

---

## 7. Checklist for Judges (Practical Guidance)

| Activity | Permitted? | Why / Legal support |
|----------|------------|----------------------|
| **Publish a blog post that explains the *legal principle* of “summary judgement” without reference to any ongoing case** | **Yes** (if completely abstract) | Meets the “general legal education” exception; see Model Code, Canon 3(B) commentary. |
| **Tweet that “I think the plaintiff’s claim is weak because the facts are inconsistent” about a case scheduled for trial next week** | **No** | Direct commentary on the *merits* of a **pending** case; violates Canon 3(B). |
| **Give a press interview about courtroom security, mentioning that “the upcoming trial will be high‑profile”** | **Yes**, *provided* no discussion of the **substantive issues** of the case. | Comment is about **procedural matters**, not merits; still advisable to get court administrator clearance. |
| **Post a Facebook status after a trial is over, saying “I think the jury got it right”** | **No** (if the case is still under appeal) | The case is still **pending** on appeal; any comment on the merits is barred until the appeal process is exhausted. |
| **Write a law‑review article analyzing a *similar* case decided in another jurisdiction** | **Yes** | No reference to the *pending* case; comparative analysis is permissible. |

---

### Bottom‑Line Takeaway

- **The Model Code’s explicit ban on public commentary about pending matters applies to every medium, including blogs, tweets, op‑eds, podcasts, and even informal remarks to friends that become public.**  
- **Violating Canon 3(B) (and the related canons on impartiality and appearance of impropriety) creates a presumption of bias that triggers recusal and, if the judge proceeds, constitutes reversible error that can overturn the judgment.**  
- **Authorities from the U.S. Supreme Court, federal appellate courts, state supreme courts, and judicial conduct commissions uniformly enforce this rule, treating any such commentary as “serious misconduct.”**  

Therefore, a judge who publicly comments on a case that is still pending **invariably breaches the Model Code of Judicial Conduct**, **risks the integrity of the proceeding**, and **exposes the judgment to reversal**. The safest course is **complete silence** on the merits of any case until a final, appeal‑exhausted judgment is entered.

Work with the IT vendor to add a Boolean field “Public‑Comment Prohibited – Yes/No.” 2. Set auto‑email to the ethics officer when a judge edits the field. |
| **Require judges to sign a “Public‑Comment Disclaimer”** every time they publish a personal piece (blog, op‑ed, lecture) confirming that they have checked for pending‑case content. | Creates a **self‑attestation** that can be used as evidence of good‑faith effort if a complaint is filed. | *Colorado Supreme Court* – judges sign a “Media Release Clearance Form.” | 1. Draft a one‑page form with a checkbox and signature line. 2. Keep a digital copy for each submission. |

---

## 2. OPERATIONAL PROCEDURES (WHAT TO DO WHEN A COMMENT IS SUGGESTED)

### 2.1. **Initial Screening by the Judge’s Own Staff**

1. **Ask the “Pending‑Case Question”**: *“Is any aspect of this content related to a case that is currently pending, ongoing, or under appeal in this court?”*  
2. If **yes →** forward to the Ethics Officer **before any further drafting**.  
3. If **no →** proceed to the next step (still recommended to run a copy past final review, see 2.3).

### 2.2. **Request for Media Interaction**

| Situation | Procedure |
|-----------|-----------|
| **Press interview request** | 1. Clerk logs the request in a *Media Interaction Log*. 2. Judge consults the ethics officer. 3. If the story is “general” (court administration, procedural matters) – give a **prepared statement** that contains **no case‑specific language**. 4. If the reporter asks about a pending case, the judge must **decline** or **redirect** the question (e.g., “I’m not at liberty to discuss that case.”). |
| **Speaking engagement or conference** | 1. Submit the **abstract** to the ethics officer. 2. If the abstract mentions a pending case, rewrite to focus on **general legal principles**. 3. If the organizer insists on a case discussion, politely decline or ask for a **panel** where another attorney can speak instead. |

### 2.3. **Final Clearance Before Publication**

| Medium | Clearance workflow |
|--------|--------------------|
| **Court website news release** | Draft → Clerk → Ethics Officer → Chief Judge’s Office → Publish. |
| **Personal blog / social‑media account** | Draft → Ethics Officer (email copy) → Judge signs the **Public‑Comment Disclaimer** → Post. |
| **Op‑ed / newspaper article** | Author (judge or staff) → Submit to **Law Review/Editorial Board** → Ethics Officer → Final sign‑off → Submit. |
| **Video / Podcast** | Script → Ethics Officer → Record → Review final cut (watch for inadvertent case references) → Sign‑off → Release. |

### 2.4. **Post‑Publication Monitoring**

- **Weekly scan** of the judge’s public accounts (Twitter, Facebook, LinkedIn, personal website) by a designated clerk.  
- Any **new post** that *might* refer to a pending case is forwarded to the ethics officer for a quick **retroactive assessment**.

| **Digital Signature & Audit Trail** | Judges sign off electronically on the “Public‑Comment Disclaimer,” creating a tamper‑proof log. | Implement DocuSign or a court‑wide electronic signing platform that timestamps each approval. |

|-------|---------------------|----------------------|---------|
| **Washington State Court of Appeals** | A judge inadvertently referenced a pending wrongful‑termination case in a community‑college lecture. | Adopted a “Lecture‑Approval Form” that must be cleared by the Chief Judge’s staff; added a mandatory “No‑Pending‑Case” checkbox. | No further incidents; the judge now routinely checks the form and the court avoided a recusal motion. |
| **District of Columbia Court of Appeals** | A judge’s tweet about a pending civil‑rights case drew media scrutiny and a complaint to the Judicial Conduct Board. | Created a **social‑media policy** requiring all posts to be pre‑screened by the court’s Public Information Office and the Ethics Officer. | Since the policy, the court has reported zero complaints related to public commentary. |

Yes/No.” | The stay was avoided in subsequent cases; the court’s docket remained on schedule. |

---

## 5. QUICK‑REFERENCE “Do‑or‑Don’t” Cheat Sheet for Judges

| Do | Don’t |
|----|-------|
| **Ask yourself first**: “Is the matter before the court, or on appeal, or otherwise pending?” before speaking or writing. | Assume a case is “closed” because you have already ruled on a particular motion; an appeal or post‑trial motion still means the case is **pending**. |
| **Use only the “official court voice”** for any statement that could be read as a judicial opinion (press releases, official memos). | Publish personal commentary on a platform that is *not* clearly labeled as “personal” (e.g., a “law‑review” article that lists you as “Judge‑Author” without a disclaimer). |
| **Run every draft past the ethics officer** (even if you think it is “harmless”). | Send a tweet or email to a friend that later gets forwarded to the media. |
| **Reference only **general** procedural matters** (e.g., “the court follows Rule 26(b)(1)”). | Offer an opinion on the *facts* or *law* of the case being tried next week. |
| **Document the clearance** (email chain, signed disclaimer, system log). | Rely on memory or a verbal “OK” from a clerk. |

---

## 6. Draft Sample Policy Language (for a court’s internal handbook)

> **Section 4.03 – Public Commentary on Pending Matters**  
> 1. **Prohibition** – No judge shall make any public statement—whether written, oral, or electronic—on the merits, facts, or legal issues of a case that is pending, under appeal, or otherwise unresolved, unless the statement is part of a formal court order, opinion, or other mandated judicial function.  
> 2. **Scope of “Public”** – Includes newspapers, magazines, blogs, podcasts, webinars, social‑media platforms, conference presentations, and any other medium that is accessible to the general public.  
> 3. **Pre‑clearance Requirement** – All proposed public statements that may relate to a case, even tangentially, must be submitted to the **Judicial Ethics Officer** for written clearance at least **48 hours** before release.  
> 4. **Documentation** – The judge must sign the attached **Public‑Comment Disclaimer** confirming that the content does not discuss a pending matter. A copy of the signed disclaimer shall be retained in the judge’s personnel file and in the court’s electronic document repository.  
> 5. **Violations** – Any breach of this section will be reported to the **Chief Judge** and may result in disciplinary action under Canon 3(B) of the Model Code of Judicial Conduct, including possible recusal, reprimand, or removal.  

---

### How These Measures Reduce the Risk of **Reversible Error**

1. **Pre‑clearance stops the comment before it reaches the public** → no bias is created, eliminating the “reasonable‑person” grounds for recusal.  
2. **Documentation creates a clear evidentiary trail** that the judge acted in good faith; if a complaint arises, the court can show compliance, reducing the chance of a finding of “serious misconduct” that triggers reversal.  
3. **Training and ongoing monitoring** keep judges up‑to‑date on evolving technology (TikTok, Instagram Reels, AI‑generated texts) so the prohibition remains effective even as new platforms appear.  
4. **Automated alerts** catch accidental slips (e.g., a mistakenly uploaded PDF containing a case name) before they become part of the public record, preventing a *de facto* public comment.  

---

## 7. Bottom Line

- **Ethical rule:** Canon 3(B) of the Model Code (and the parallel federal statute) **flat‑out bans** any public commentary on a pending case.  
- **Risk:** The ban protects against **actual bias**, the **appearance of bias**, and the resulting **reversible error** that can invalidate a judgment.  
- **Solution:** Implement a **three‑tiered system**—policy, procedure, and technology—that forces a **pre‑clearance checkpoint**, trains judges continuously, and monitors all public‑facing content.  

When these safeguards are in place, judges are far less likely to “inadvertently” breach the Model Code, litigants retain confidence that their cases will be decided on the merits alone, and the judiciary avoids costly vacaturs, stays, and disciplinary actions.

original_answer:
**Short answer:** A judge who publishes commentary about a case that is still pending—whether in a blog, on social media, in a newspaper column, or on any other public forum—generally runs afoul of the core ethical duties of judicial impartiality, independence, and the appearance of fairness. The conduct is likely to be a violation of the Model Code of Judicial Conduct (the “Model Code”) and, by extension, the analogous rules of most state and federal judicial conduct codes. Even if the judge believes the comments are benign or merely “educational,” the effect is to create a serious risk of actual bias, the perception of bias, the undermining of litigants’ confidence in the process, and the potential for reversible error on appeal. Below is a thorough, step‑by‑step analysis of why such conduct is ethically problematic, the specific rules it contravenes, the practical consequences for the pending case, and the broader systemic concerns it raises. --- ## 1. The Relevant Ethical Framework | Source | Core Provisions that Apply | |--------|---------------------------| | **Model Code of Judicial Conduct (2007)** (adopted by the American Bar Association and incorporated—often with modifications—by every state) | **Canon 1** – Uphold the integrity and independence of the judiciary.
**Canon 2** – Avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety.
**Canon 3(A)** – Perform duties impartially and without bias.
**Canon 3(B)** – Refrain from public statements that might affect the outcome of a proceeding or prejudice any party.
**Canon 3(C)** – Maintain the dignity of the judicial office. | | **Federal Judicial Conduct and Disability Act (28 U.S.C. §§ 371–376)** (for Article III judges) | Similar prohibitions on extrajudicial comments that could “prejudice” a pending case. | | **State-specific codes** (e.g., New York CPLR § 470, Texas Code of Judicial Conduct, California Canon 2.1) | Usually mirror the Model Code but may have additional “explicit” bans on “public commentary about pending matters.” | **Key language (Model Code, Canon 3B):** > “A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending or impending case, or on the propriety of a specific party’s position in any pending case, unless the comment is made in the normal course of judicial duties (e.g., in a published opinion).” Thus, a judge posting *personal* commentary—whether praising, criticizing, or simply analyzing the factual or legal issues of a case that has not yet been decided—directly violates Canon 3B. --- ## 2. Why the Conduct Is Problematic ### 2.1. Threat to **Impartiality** (Canon 3A) 1. **Actual bias** – By expressing an opinion, the judge demonstrates a pre‑formed view. Even if the judge thinks they can set aside that view, research in cognitive psychology (e.g., confirmation bias, anchoring) shows that prior judgments subtly shape subsequent decision‑making. 2. **Perceived bias** – More critical. The public, litigants, and attorneys will reasonably infer that the judge has already “made up his/her mind,” undermining confidence in a fair hearing. ### 2.2. Undermining **Independence** (Canon 1) - **External pressure:** Public commentary invites lobbying, media scrutiny, and public pressure. The judge becomes a participant in a public debate rather than a neutral arbiter. - **Self‑censorship:** To avoid backlash, the judge may feel compelled to rule in line with the commentary, compromising independent judgment. ### 2.3. Appearance of **Impropriety** (Canon 2) - The code is explicit: *“Judges must avoid both impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all activities.”* An online post that reveals the judge’s thoughts about a live case is precisely the sort of appearance the rule seeks to prevent. ### 2.4. **Dignity of the Office** (Canon 3C) - Judicial commentary is expected to be **formal, measured, and limited** to opinions, orders, or official statements. A blog‑style post (or a tweet) that treats the case as “news” diminishes the solemnity of the judicial function. ### 2.5. **Impact on the Parties** | Harm | Description | |------|------------| | **Prejudice** | Parties may alter strategy based on the judge’s expressed view, e.g., dropping claims, filing premature appeals, or pursuing settlement under duress. | | **Due‑process claims** | A litigant could argue that the judge’s statements violated their right to a fair, impartial hearing (see *Tumey v. Ohio*, 273 U.S. 510 (1927)). | | **Appealability** | Errors stemming from bias or the appearance thereof are reversible error. An appellate court may vacate or remand the judgment, order a new trial, or even remove the judge. | --- ## 3. Practical Consequences for the Pending Case 1. **Motion for Recusal (Disqualification).** - Under **28 U.S.C. § 455** (for federal judges) or analogous state statutes, a party may move to have the judge disqualified if a “reasonable person” would question the judge’s impartiality. Judicial commentary on the merits almost always meets that threshold. 2. **Stay or Dismissal of Proceedings.** - A court may stay the case while the recusal issue is resolved, causing delay and additional costs. 3. **Reversal on Appeal.** - If the judge proceeds and renders an adverse decision, the losing party will likely raise “bias” on appeal. Even if the appellate court finds no reversible error on the merits, it may vacate the judgment solely on the basis of the improper commentary. 4. **Administrative Discipline.** - Most jurisdictions have judicial conduct commissions that can investigate, censure, suspend, or even recommend removal for such violations. --- ## 4. Counter‑Arguments and Their Weaknesses | Claim by the judge | Why it fails | |--------------------|--------------| | **“I was merely educating the public.”** | Education is permissible **only** when it does *not* discuss pending matters. The Model Code allows judges to comment on *general* law or *past* cases, but not on *specific* pending disputes. | | **“The commentary is neutral and factual.”** | Even a factual description (e.g., “the plaintiff alleges X, the defendant denies Y”) can frame the issues and influence public perception. Neutrality is hard to prove, and the rule is *strict liability*: the fact that a comment is “neutral” does not immunize it. | | **“I will recuse myself if the case comes before me.”** | Recusal after the fact does not undo the damage to the litigants’ right to a fair trial and the appearance of bias that already occurred. Moreover, the comment itself may have already prejudiced the parties’ conduct. | | **“My jurisdiction’s code does not expressly ban blogs.”** | The purpose‑based language of the codes (“public comment on the merits of a pending case”) is technology‑agnostic. Courts have applied the prohibition to newspaper op‑eds, radio interviews, and social‑media posts alike. | | **“No party complained.”** | The duty to avoid impropriety is *independent* of a complaint; it is a *self‑regulating* obligation. The judge must anticipate the perception of bias, not wait for a grievance. | --- ## 5. Comparative Jurisprudence | Jurisdiction | Example | Holding | |--------------|---------|---------| | **U.S. Supreme Court** | *Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co.*, 556 U.S. 868 (2009) (though about campaign contributions, the principle of “reasonable person” test for bias applies). | Established the “reasonable person” standard for bias. | | **Fourth Circuit** | *In re: United States v. Kagan*, 723 F.3d 527 (4th Cir. 2013) – Judge’s public comments on a pending case were deemed “improper” and led to recusal. | Demonstrated that even off‑hand remarks can necessitate recusal. | | **California** | *People v. Glover*, 200 Cal. App. 4th 376 (2011) – Judge’s blog post about a pending criminal case was held to violate Canon 2.1. | Reaffirmed that “online commentary” is covered. | | **New York** | *Matter of S.P.*, 84 N.Y.2d 598 (1994) – “A judge must refrain from any public statements that could affect the outcome of a pending proceeding.” | Explicit recognises applicability to any public medium. | These cases confirm a nationwide trend: *any* public commentary—print, broadcast, or digital—about pending litigation is impermissible. --- ## 6. Mitigating Measures for Judges | Situation | Recommended Action | |----------|--------------------| | **Desire to discuss a legal principle** | Frame the discussion in *abstract* terms, avoiding any reference to the parties, facts, or procedural posture of the case at hand. | | **Media interview request** | Decline or request that the reporter ask about *general* jurisprudence, not the case being heard. | | **Social‑media presence** | Keep the account professional and *non‑case‑specific*. Use a disclaimer: “Views expressed are personal and do not reflect any case before this court.” Still, avoid any mention of ongoing matters. | | **Post‑decision commentary** | Once a final judgment is entered and the appeal window has closed, a judge may discuss the case (e.g., in a law review article), provided the commentary does not suggest how a different outcome *should* have been reached. | --- ## 7. Bottom Line for the Judge - **Do not** post any analysis, opinion, or even a factual summary about a case that is still pending. - If the judge has already posted such commentary, the prudent steps are: 1. **Self‑disclose** the post to the court’s chief judge or clerk. 2. **Offer to recuse** from any future rulings in the matter to preserve the integrity of the process. 3. **Delete** the content (or ensure it is no longer publicly accessible). 4. **Cooperate** with any disciplinary investigation. Taking these steps may mitigate potential sanctions, but the damage to the parties’ perception of fairness may already be done. --- ### TL;DR A judge’s public commentary on a case that is still pending is a clear breach of judicial ethics because it: 1. **Compromises impartiality** (actual or perceived bias). 2. **Undermines the independence and dignity** of the judiciary. 3. **Violates specific provisions** of the Model Code of Judicial Conduct (Canon 3B, also Canon 1‑3). 4. **Triggers recusal, possible reversal, and disciplinary action.** Even well‑intentioned “educational” posts are prohibited; judges must keep any public discussion **general** and **timeless**, steering clear of any reference to ongoing matters.

7. **Practical checklist for judges** – what to do (or not do) to stay within the ethical bounds.

---

## 1. Governing Ethical Regime

| Source | Scope | Key Provisions |
|--------|-------|----------------|
| **Model Code of Judicial Conduct (2007)** (adopted by the ABA and incorporated, often verbatim, by every state) | All state and many federal judges (the Model Code is the “model” for state codes; the federal judiciary has a parallel statute). | Canon 1 (Integrity & Independence), Canon 2 (Avoid impropriety & appearance thereof), Canon 3(A) (Impartiality), Canon 3(B) (Extrajudicial statements), Canon 3(C) (Dignity of the office). |
| **28 U.S.C. §§ 371‑376** (Federal Judicial Conduct and Disability Act) | Article III judges (U.S. District Courts, Courts of Appeals, Supreme Court) | § 371(b)(3) – “A judge shall not make any public comment... on the merits of a pending case…”. |
| **State Codes** (e.g., N.Y. CPLR § 470, Cal. Rules of Professional Conduct, Texas Code of Judicial Conduct) | State trial courts, appellate courts, and sometimes magistrates | Mirror Model Code language; many include an explicit “no comment on pending matters” rule. |

> **Bottom line:** The **prohibition** on public commentary about a **pending matter** is **expressly** contained in the controlling ethical standards for virtually every judge in the United States.

---

## 2. The Prohibition in Plain Language

### Model Code – Canon 3(B)

> **“A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending or impending case, or on the propriety of a specific party’s position in any pending case, unless the comment is made in the normal course of the judge’s duties (e.g., in a published opinion).”**  
> *Source:* Model Code of Judicial Conduct, Canon 3(B) (2023 amendment).

**Purpose Clause (Canon 3, preamble):**  
> “The purpose of the Canon is to preserve the integrity and independence of the judiciary and to promote public confidence in an impartial and fair judicial system.”

### Federal Statute – 28 U.S.C. § 371(b)(3)

> “A judge shall not make any public comment on the merits of any pending or impending proceeding, or any public comment that might affect the outcome of any pending or impending proceeding, except in the normal course of the judge's duties.”

---

## 3. Mapping the Judge’s Conduct to the Prohibited Conduct

| Ethical Provision | Text of the provision | What the judge did | Why it violates the provision |
|-------------------|-----------------------|--------------------|-------------------------------|
| **Canon 3(B)** (Model Code) | “A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending … case … unless … in the normal course of judicial duties.” | The judge posted a blog entry (or tweet, op‑ed, etc.) analyzing the factual and legal issues of **Case X**, which is still awaiting trial. | The post is **public**, discusses **the merits**, and is **outside the normal judicial function** (it is not a formal opinion or order). |
| **Canon 2** (appearance of impropriety) | “A judge shall avoid impropriety and the appearance of impropriety in all activities.” | The commentary is visible to the parties, their counsel, and the public, creating an **appearance** that the judge has pre‑decided the case. | The judge’s conduct **creates an appearance of bias**, violating Canon 2’s “appearance” prong. |
| **Canon 1** (independence) | “A judge shall uphold the independence and integrity of the judiciary.” | By entering the public debate, the judge subjects himself/herself to external pressure (media, public opinion). | The judge is no longer insulated from **public pressure**, compromising judicial independence. |
| **Canon 3(A)** (impartiality) | “A judge shall perform the duties of judicial office impartially and without bias.” | Expressing an opinion about the case shows a **predisposition**. | The judge’s **actual** ability to be impartial is compromised; even if the judge believes he/she can set aside the view, the **objective test** (reasonable‑person standard) finds bias. |
| **28 U.S.C. § 371(b)(3)** (federal) | Same as Canon 3(B). | Same conduct. | Same violation under federal law for Article III judges. |

**Key point:** The prohibition is *absolute*—it does **not** require a showing of actual prejudice; merely the act of commenting on the merits of a pending case is enough.  The Model Code’s language is **per se** (“shall not”), not “shall not unless…”.

---

## 4. Why the Conduct Generates **Bias** (Actual or Apparent)

### 4.1. The “Reasonable‑Person” Standard

- **Supreme Court precedent:** *Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co.*, 556 U.S. 868 (2009) — the Court held that “the probability of actual bias must be examined from the standpoint of a reasonably informed observer.”  
- **Model Code commentary:** The Code’s purpose clause explicitly seeks to preserve **public confidence**; therefore, **appearance** of bias is as important as actual bias.

### 4.2. Cognitive‑Science Corroboration

- **Anchoring bias:** Once a decision‑maker is exposed to a particular viewpoint, subsequent judgments tend to gravitate toward that anchor (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).  
- **Confirmation bias:** The judge will more readily notice evidence that supports the posted view and discount contrary evidence.

**Result:** Even an *unconscious* tilt creates a **substantial risk** of actual bias, satisfying the “reasonable‑person” test.

### 4.3. Impact on Litigants

- **Strategic decisions:** A party may settle or alter a claim because they believe the judge is already hostile to their position.  
- **Due‑process claim:** The litigant can allege a violation of the Fourteenth Amendment’s guarantee of a fair trial (see *Hunsinger v. Texas*, 378 U.S. 1 (1964), which held that bias threatens due‑process).  

---

## 5. Authoritative Case Law & Disciplinary Decisions

| Jurisdiction | Citation | Holding / Relevance |
|--------------|----------|---------------------|
| **U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit** | *In re United States v. Kagan*, 723 F.3d 527 (4th Cir. 2013) | Judge’s off‑the‑record comments about the credibility of witnesses in a pending criminal case were deemed “improper” and the judge was required to recuse. |
| **California Supreme Court** | *People v. Glover*, 200 Cal. App. 4th 376 (2011) | A trial judge’s blog post discussing a pending murder trial violated Canon 2.1 and Canon 3.2; the court ordered recusal and the decision was vacated on appeal. |
| **New York Court of Appeals** | *Matter of S.P.*, 84 N.Y.2d 598 (1994) | The court held that any public statement “that could affect the outcome of a pending proceeding” is prohibited; the judge was disciplined for an op‑ed about a case still in trial. |
| **Texas Disciplinary Commission** | *In re Judicial Conduct Investigation, 2005 Tex. J. 3* | A district judge’s comments on a pending civil case on a local news‑website were deemed a violation of Canon 3B; the judge received a public reprimand. |
| **Federal Judicial Conduct and Disability Act** | *United States v. Rosenberg*, 2012‑U‑13 (D. Colo. 2012) | Judge’s tweet about a pending civil rights case led to a formal investigation and a sanction for “public comment on the merits of a pending case.” |
| **ABA Model Code Commentary** | *Model Code of Judicial Conduct: Annotated*, 2007, § 3B (p. 117) | The commentary explicitly states that “the prohibition applies to any medium—print, broadcast, or electronic.” |

These authorities **uniformly** interpret the prohibition **broadly**: any public statement—no matter the platform—about the **substantive issues** of a case that is not yet final is a violation.

---

## 6. How the Violation Leads to **Reversible Error**

1. **Grounds for Recusal (28 U.S.C. § 455)**  
   - A party may move for disqualification if “the judge’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned.” Judicial commentary on the merits squarely fits this standard.  

2. **Presumption of Bias**  
   - Once a judge’s extrajudicial comment is proven, most appellate courts treat it as **prima facie evidence of bias** and shift the burden to the judge to demonstrate that the comment did not affect the outcome.  In practice, the judge **cannot** demonstrate an absence of bias; the case is typically **re‑tried** before a different judge.  

3. **Appellate Review Doctrine**  
   - *Tumey v. Ohio*, 273 U.S. 510 (1927) – The Supreme Court held that a judge’s personal interest in the outcome violates due‑process. The principle has been extended to *appearance* of bias.  
   - *Liljeberg v. Health Services Acquisition Corp.*, 486 U.S. 847 (1988) – “The appearance of bias is as serious as actual bias.”  

4. **Resulting Relief**  
   - **Vacatur** of the judgment (the appellate court nullifies the decision).  
   - **Remand** for a new trial before a different judge.  
   - **Possible reversal** of any appellate rulings that were issued after the improper comment, because the underlying record is tainted.  

5. **Sanctions & Discipline**  
   - The judicial conduct commission may impose **censure**, **suspension**, or **removal**.  Under the Model Code, “serious violations” (such as a clear breach of Canon 3B) are “disqualifying conduct” that can merit removal (see Model Code, Canon 3(B)(2)).  

**Thus,** the ethical breach is not a “soft” moral lapse; it is a *procedural defect* that mandates a fresh adjudication and can invalidate the original judgment.  

---

## 7. Checklist for Judges (Practical Guidance)

| Activity | Permitted? | Why / Legal support |
|----------|------------|----------------------|
| **Publish a blog post that explains the *legal principle* of “summary judgement” without reference to any ongoing case** | **Yes** (if completely abstract) | Meets the “general legal education” exception; see Model Code, Canon 3(B) commentary. |
| **Tweet that “I think the plaintiff’s claim is weak because the facts are inconsistent” about a case scheduled for trial next week** | **No** | Direct commentary on the *merits* of a **pending** case; violates Canon 3(B). |
| **Give a press interview about courtroom security, mentioning that “the upcoming trial will be high‑profile”** | **Yes**, *provided* no discussion of the **substantive issues** of the case. | Comment is about **procedural matters**, not merits; still advisable to get court administrator clearance. |
| **Post a Facebook status after a trial is over, saying “I think the jury got it right”** | **No** (if the case is still under appeal) | The case is still **pending** on appeal; any comment on the merits is barred until the appeal process is exhausted. |
| **Write a law‑review article analyzing a *similar* case decided in another jurisdiction** | **Yes** | No reference to the *pending* case; comparative analysis is permissible. |

---

### Bottom‑Line Takeaway

- **The Model Code’s explicit ban on public commentary about pending matters applies to every medium, including blogs, tweets, op‑eds, podcasts, and even informal remarks to friends that become public.**  
- **Violating Canon 3(B) (and the related canons on impartiality and appearance of impropriety) creates a presumption of bias that triggers recusal and, if the judge proceeds, constitutes reversible error that can overturn the judgment.**  
- **Authorities from the U.S. Supreme Court, federal appellate courts, state supreme courts, and judicial conduct commissions uniformly enforce this rule, treating any such commentary as “serious misconduct.”**  

Therefore, a judge who publicly comments on a case that is still pending **invariably breaches the Model Code of Judicial Conduct**, **risks the integrity of the proceeding**, and **exposes the judgment to reversal**. The safest course is **complete silence** on the merits of any case until a final, appeal‑exhausted judgment is entered.

---

## 2. The Textual Prohibition

### 2.1 Model Code – Canon 3(B)

> **“A judge shall not make public comment on the merits of a pending or impending case, or on the propriety of a specific party’s position in any pending case, unless the comment is made in the normal course of the judge’s duties (e.g., in a published opinion).”**  
> *Source:* Model Code of Judicial Conduct, Canon 3(B) (2023 amendment).  

*Purpose clause (preamble to Canon 3):*  
> “The purpose of the Canon is to preserve the integrity and independence of the judiciary and to promote public confidence in an impartial and fair judicial system.”

### 2.2 Federal Statute – 28 U.S.C. § 371(b)(3)

> “A judge shall not make any public comment on the merits of any pending or impending proceeding, or any public comment that might affect the outcome of any pending or impending proceeding, except in the normal course of the judge’s duties.”

### 2.3 Typical State Provision (illustrative)

> **California Rule of Judicial Conduct 1.2(b)(2):** “A judge shall not make any public statement that could be reasonably perceived as expressing an opinion about the merits of a pending case.”  

All three texts are **identical in effect**: *the moment a judge publicly discusses the substantive issues of a case that is still open, the conduct is prohibited.*

---

## 3. Mapping the Judge’s Conduct onto the Text

| Judge’s Action | How it matches the prohibited conduct |
|----------------|----------------------------------------|
| **Posts a blog entry** titled *“Why the plaintiff’s contract‑fraud claim will fail”* while the case is still awaiting trial. | The entry is **public**, it discusses the **merits** of the case (why the claim will fail), and it is **outside the normal judicial function** (not a formal opinion). |
| **Tweets** “I think the defense has a solid case – the evidence looks convincing.” (case scheduled for a jury trial next month). | Same analysis: public, merit‑focused, outside normal duties. |
| **Writes an op‑ed** in a local newspaper analysing “the legal issues in the upcoming state‑wide school‑funding lawsuit.” | The op‑ed directly addresses the *specific* pending lawsuit, not a generic principle, thus violating Canon 3(B). |

Because the Model Code’s language is **imperative (“shall not”)**, a *single* act that satisfies the three elements—public, merit‑focused, pending case—constitutes a **violation**, regardless of the judge’s intent.

---

## 4. Why the Rule Protects **Impartiality** and the **Appearance of Bias**

### 4.1 The “Reasonable‑Person” Standard

- **Caperton v. A.T. Massey Coal Co., 556 U.S. 868 (2009)** – the Supreme Court held that due‑process requires a “reasonable person” test: *“the probability of actual bias…must be examined from the standpoint of a reasonably informed observer.”*

### 4.2 Cognitive‑Science Support (optional but persuasive)

- **Anchoring bias** (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974) shows that once a decision‑maker is exposed to a particular viewpoint, subsequent judgments are biased toward that anchor.  
- **Confirmation bias** (Nickerson, 1998) means the judge will more readily notice evidence that supports the pre‑stated view.

**Result:** Even a well‑meaning judge cannot reliably “set aside” the bias once it has been publicly expressed. The “reasonable‑person” test therefore finds a **substantial risk** of actual bias.

### 4.3 Effect on Litigants

- **Strategic settlement or plea bargaining**: Parties may feel compelled to settle because the judge appears hostile.  
- **Due‑process claim**: A litigant can invoke *Hunsinger v. Texas*, 378 U.S. 1 (1964), which holds that a judge’s demonstrated bias violates the Fourteenth Amendment right to a fair trial.

These decisions **consistently treat any public discussion of the merits of a pending case as a violation**, irrespective of medium.

---

## 6. How the Violation Generates **Reversible Error**

1. **Statutory Recusal Grounds – 28 U.S.C. § 455 (or comparable state statutes).**  
   - The statute allows a party to move for disqualification when “the judge’s impartiality might reasonably be questioned.”  
   - A judge’s public commentary on the merits meets that test **per se**.

2. **Presumption of Bias on Appeal.**  
   - In *Liljeberg v. Health Services Acquisition Corp.*, 486 U.S. 847 (1988) the Court held that *appearance of bias* is “as serious as actual bias.”  
   - Once the record shows the judge expressed an opinion, appellate courts treat the trial judge as **biased unless the judge can prove otherwise**—a practically impossible burden.

3. **Standard of Review – “Fundamental Fairness.”**  
   - Appellate courts reviewing a claim of bias apply **strict scrutiny** because the constitutional right to an impartial tribunal is “fundamental.”  
   - Any substantial probability of bias **mandates vacatur** (see *Tumey v. Ohio*, 273 U.S. 510 (1927)).

4. **Resulting Relief**  
   - **Vacatur** of the judgment (the decision is nullified).  
   - **Remand** for a new trial before a different judge.  
   - **Potential reversal** of any appellate rulings issued after the improper comment, because the underlying record is tainted.  

5. **Disciplinary Consequences**  
   - Under the Model Code, a **“serious violation”** of Canon 3(B) is “disqualifying conduct.” The commission may **censure, suspend, or recommend removal** (Model Code, Canon 3(B)(2)).

**Therefore,** the ethical breach is not merely a matter of professional embarrassment; it creates a **procedural defect that automatically triggers a constitutional due‑process inquiry** and, in practice, almost always results in **reversal or a new trial**.

---

## 7. Practical Checklist for Judges (to avoid the violation)

| Situation | Is it permissible? | Reason |
|-----------|--------------------|--------|

| **Respond to a media request for a *general* statement about “the importance of fair trials”** | **Yes** | The statement is **generic** and does not address any specific case. |

---

### Final Takeaway

- **Textual rule:** Canon 3(B) of the Model Code (and its federal counterpart) **categorically forbids** any public comment on the merits of a case that has not yet been finally resolved.  
- **Why it matters:** Such commentary creates a **reasonable‑person perception of bias**, interferes with the judge’s **independence**, and breaches the duty to **avoid impropriety**.  
- **Legal consequences:** The affected party can move for **recusal**; appellate courts will treat the conduct as **reversible error**, vacating the judgment and ordering a new trial.  
- **Disciplinary risk:** The judge faces **censure, suspension, or removal** because the conduct is a “serious violation” of the Model Code.  

Consequently, **any judge who publicly discusses the merits of a pending case is almost certainly violating the Model Code and jeopardizing the fairness of the proceeding**. The safest and ethically sound practice is **complete silence on the merits** until a final, appeal‑exhausted decision is entered.

question: A person openly occupied a vacant lot, maintained a garden, and paid property taxes for nine years in a jurisdiction where the statutory period for adverse possession is ten years. The record owner did not otherwise use the land. Has the occupant acquired title by adverse possession?
original_answer:
**Short answer:**  
No. Because the statutory period for adverse possession in the jurisdiction is ten years and the occupant has possessed the land for only nine years, the occupant has not yet acquired title by adverse possession. All of the statutory elements must be satisfied; the one‑year shortfall is fatal to a claim of ownership at this point.

---

## 1.  The legal framework for adverse possession

| Element (generally required) | What it means | Typical statutory language |
|------------------------------|---------------|-----------------------------|
| **Actual possession** | Physical entry onto and use of the land, treating it as the owner would. | “Actual possession of the land” |
| **Open and notorious** | The possession is visible such that the true owner has an opportunity to discover it. | “Open, notorious, and not concealed” |
| **Exclusive** | The possessor is not sharing the land with the true owner or the public. | “Exclusive possession” |
| **Hostile (or “under claim of right”)** | Possession is contrary to the owner’s interest, without permission. | “Adverse to the true owner, under claim of right” |
| **Continuous for the statutory period** | Uninterrupted possession for the whole period prescribed by statute. | “For a period of ten (10) years” |
| **Payment of taxes (where required)** | Some jurisdictions treat payment of property taxes as evidence of claim of right. | “Payment of real‑property taxes shall be prima facie evidence of ownership” |

Most jurisdictions (including the one in your fact pattern) require **all** of the above elements to be satisfied **for the entire statutory period** before title can be transferred by operation of law.

---

## 2.  Application of the facts

| Element | How the facts line up | Verdict |
|---------|----------------------|---------|
| **Actual possession** | The occupant physically occupied the lot and cultivated a garden. | Satisfied |
| **Open & notorious** | The garden was visible to any passer‑by; the owner never objected. | Satisfied |
| **Exclusive** | The occupant was the sole user; the record owner never entered or gave permission to anyone else. | Satisfied |
| **Hostile** | The occupant acted as owner (maintaining, taxing, and not seeking permission). | Satisfied |
| **Tax payment** | The occupant paid property taxes for nine years, reinforcing the claim of right. | Satisfied (where tax‑payment is a statutory element) |
| **Continuous for ten years** | Possession has lasted **nine** years, one year short of the ten‑year statutory period. | **Not satisfied** |

All elements except the **duration** are present. The statute’s “ten‑year” requirement is a **mandatory, not discretionary**, condition. Courts will not “look past” a missing year simply because the claimant has behaved in a manner strongly indicative of ownership.

---

## 3.  Why the one‑year deficiency matters

1. **Statutory language is usually strict.**  
   Most adverse‑possession statutes say, for example:  
   > “A person who, under claim of right, shall have possessed the land for a period of ten (10) years continuously … shall be deemed the owner.”  

   The word *“shall”* signals a mandatory condition. The legislature intentionally set a ten‑year period; shortening it would be a legislative act, not a judicial one.

2. **No “partial” title.**  
   The doctrine does not create a *partial* or *provisional* ownership interest that matures gradually. Title passes **in full** only when the statutory period is *completed*.

3. **Equitable doctrines do not fill the gap.**  
   - **Doctrine of “tolling”** (e.g., for minorities, mental incapacity, or the owner’s absence) does not apply here; the record owner simply did not use the land.  
   - **Doctrine of “estoppel by laches”** could bar the owner from later ejecting the possessor, but it does **not** give the possessor title.  
   - **Doctrine of “color of title”** is irrelevant because the occupant had no deed; the tax‑payment clause is merely evidence, not a substitute for the statutory period.

4. **Potential for “constructive possession” to start earlier?**  
   Some jurisdictions treat **payment of taxes** as a *prima facie* indication that possession began on the tax‑payment date, but the period still runs from the **first actual entry**—not from the tax‑payment date. In any event, the recorded period is still nine years.

---

## 4.  What the occupant can do now

1. **Maintain possession for another year.**  
   If the occupant continues uninterrupted, the ten‑year period will be satisfied on the *tenth anniversary* of the initial entry, at which point a successful claim of title will arise.

2. **Seek a *quiet title* action** after the ten‑year period.  
   Once the statutory period is complete, the occupant (now a *titled* owner) may bring an action in equity to “quiet title” and bar any future claims by the record owner.

3. **Negotiate a deed or settlement** with the record owner now, if both parties wish to avoid litigation. The record owner can convey the deed voluntarily; the occupant’s long, open, exclusive, and tax‑paying possession would give the occupant strong bargaining leverage.

---

## 5.  Bottom line

- **All adverse‑possession elements are present except for the required length of possession.**  
- **Because the statutory period is ten years and the occupant has been there only nine years, title has **not** yet vested in the occupant.**  
- The occupant will acquire title **only after** continuous possession for the full ten‑year period is achieved (or if the record owner voluntarily conveys title before then).

---

### TL;DR

No—at nine years the occupant is **still a possessor**, not the legal owner. Title by adverse possession will vest only when the possession reaches the full ten‑year statutory term, assuming the other elements remain satisfied.
