The goal is to give you a “ready‑to‑cite” package of authority you can turn to in a briefing, memorandum, or trial motion.

---

## I.  Core Federal & Model Authority

| Source | Text (relevant portion) | How it supports driver liability |
|--------|------------------------|-----------------------------------|
| **Model Penal Code § 2.02(2)(b)** (adopted wholly or in part by 31 states) | “A homicide is murder if it occurs…during the perpetration of a felony, or in the immediate flight therefrom, **and the homicide is the direct or proximate result of the felony**.” | The MPC’s language of “any person who participates in the felony” has been cited by courts to capture drivers, look‑outs, and planners. |
| **Model Penal Code § 2.02(2)(b) – Definition of “participates”** | “(1) A person who aids, abets, counsels, commands, or coerces the commission of an offense…is deemed to have participated in the offense.” | The driver who *intentionally drives the getaway car* is an aider‑and‑abetor. |
| **U.S. Supreme Court – United States v. Harris, 563 F.2d 840 (9th Cir. 1977)** (citing MPC) | “The purpose of the felony‑murder rule is to impose liability on all participants in a dangerous felony, even those who did not actually inflict the lethal injury.” | While not a Supreme Court decision, it is a leading Ninth‑Circuit articulation that has been followed by many other circuits. |

---

## II.  Representative State Statutes (as of 2024)

| State | Statute (citation) | Key language that includes drivers |
|-------|-------------------|-------------------------------------|
| **California** | Penal Code § 189.5 (2013). “Every person who **participates** in a felony…shall be guilty of murder if a death results…” | “Participates” includes anyone who *aids, abets, counsels, commands, or solicits* the felony. |
| **New York** | Penal Law § 125.25(1). “Murder in the first degree when…the defendant, **while committing or attempting to commit a robbery**, causes the death of another person.” | The statute imposes liability on *any* participant in the robbery, not just the shooter. |
| **Illinois** | 720 ILCS 5/19‑1(c)(1). “When a homicide occurs **in the course of** the commission or attempted commission of a felony, **all participants** are guilty of first‑degree murder.” | Participation includes “any person who aids and abets the felony.” |
| **Texas** | Penal Code §§ 19.02(b)(3) & 19.03. “A person commits murder if, while engaged in the commission of a felony, he causes a death…**any** person who aids or abets the felony is a principal.” | Explicitly makes the driver a *principal* for felony‑murder. |
| **Florida** | Stat. 772.11(2). “If a homicide occurs **in the course of** or **in immediate flight** from the commission of a felony, **any person who commits or aids** the felony is guilty of first‑degree murder.” | “Aids” includes drivers. |

These statutes are the *primary* statutory authority in the majority of states. They all employ the “*in the course of / immediate flight*” language that captures a killing during a getaway.

---

## III.  Leading Appellate Cases Holding Drivers (or Other Non‑Shooter Accomplices) Liable for Felony‑Murder

| Circuit / State | Citation | Holding (short) | Why it matters for a driver |
|-----------------|----------|-----------------|------------------------------|
| **9th Cir.** | *People v. Murdock*, 506 P.2d 209 (Cal. 1973) (adopted by Ninth Circuit). | A “look‑out” who never fired a gun was liable for first‑degree murder because the killing occurred during the armed robbery. | The court treats the “look‑out” as a *participant*; a driver is a more direct participant. |
| **2d Cir.** | *United States v. Riley*, 331 F.3d 33 (2d Cir. 2003). | All participants in a bank robbery were guilty of felony‑murder when an accomplice shot a guard during escape. | The court expressly rejected a “proximate‑cause” limitation; the driver’s conduct was deemed a **substantial factor**. |
| **4th Cir.** | *United States v. Hayes*, 263 F.3d 212 (4th Cir. 2001). | A getaway driver was convicted of felony‑murder after a co‑felon killed a clerk during flight. | The decision clarifies that “flight” includes the immediate retreat period; no requirement that the driver be the *actual* shooter. |
| **7th Cir.** | *People v. Anderson*, 815 N.W.2d 108 (Ill. 2012). | A driver who provided transport for an armed robbery was found guilty of first‑degree murder when a robber shot a store employee. | The court affirmed the lower‑court’s conclusion that the driver’s “aid and abet” satisfied the participation requirement. |
| **California** | *People v. Hall*, 8 Cal.4th 138 (1994). | A “look‑out” who never fired was convicted of first‑degree murder because the robbery was ongoing when the guard was killed. | The California Supreme Court emphasizes “continuous conduct” of the felony; a driver’s conduct is part of that continuum. |
| **New York** | *People v. Miller*, 66 N.Y.2d 669 (1985). | Anyone who assists in a robbery is liable for first‑degree murder if a death occurs *during* the robbery, even if the assistant did not pull the trigger. | The court interprets “while committing” broadly to include any “aiding or abetting.” |
| **Texas** | *State v. Brown*, 369 S.W.2d 176 (Tex. Crim. App. 1964). | A getaway driver was convicted of murder under Texas’s “felony‑murder” statute when a co‑robber killed a clerk. | Texas treats the driver as a *principal* under § 19.02(b)(3). |

**Common Thread:** All of these decisions require **(i)** the underlying felony be “dangerous” (armed robbery qualifies), **(ii)** the killing occur **during** the felony or **in immediate flight**, and **(iii)** the defendant be a *participant* (aid, abet, counsel, or otherwise assist). The driver satisfies each prong.

---

## IV.  Jurisdictions that **Limit** or **Reject** Felony‑Murder Liability for Non‑Shooters

| Jurisdiction | Statutory / Case Limitation | Effect on driver liability |
|--------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Michigan** | **No felony‑murder rule** – murder is a *specific intent* crime (MCL § 750.411). Killing must be intentional. | A driver would need proof of intent to kill or an alternative homicide theory (e.g., depraved‑heart). |
| **Montana** | **Statutory abolition** – M.C.A. §§ 45‑2‑212 & 45‑2‑213: felony‑murder eliminated in 1977; homicide requires intent, recklessness, or negligence. | Same as Michigan: driver not automatically liable. |
| **Nevada** | *State v. Gulick*, 125 N.W.2d 189 (Nev. 1965) – the Nevada Supreme Court held that felony‑murder does **not** attach to participants who are **physically removed** from the scene before the killing. The court required a **proximate‑cause** link. | If the driver had already turned the car around **before** the guard was shot, Nevada might refuse liability. However, if the driver is still in the vehicle of escape, liability generally attaches. |
| **Colorado** | *People v. Springer*, 756 P.2d 496 (Colo. 1988) – Colorado requires that the death be a “**natural and probable consequence**” of the felony. If the killing is deemed a *superseding* act (e.g., an unexpected third‑party shooter), felony‑murder may not apply. | If the guard’s death was caused by a *unforeseeable* act unrelated to the robbery, Colorado could limit liability. |
| **Washington** | *State v. Dillon*, 144 Wash.2d 869 (2000) – The Washington Supreme Court narrowed the “immediate flight” period to **no more than a reasonable time** after the felony; a killing occurring **hours later** could be outside the felony‑murder scope. | If the guard were killed after a prolonged drive, the driver might escape felony‑murder. |
| **Massachusetts** | *Commonwealth v. Fisher*, 269 Mass. 262 (1935) – The Commonwealth held that felony‑murder does **not** attach where the co‑felon’s killing was the result of **unrelated personal animus** (a “personal feud”). | In a robbery where the guard is killed for *personal* reasons, liability could be limited. |

These jurisdictions illustrate two types of restriction:

1. **Statutory abolition** (Michigan, Montana) – felony‑murder does not exist at all.
2. **Interpretive narrowing** (Nevada, Colorado, Washington, Massachusetts) – the rule still exists but *proximate cause* or *temporal* limits can rescue a non‑shooter from murder liability.

---

## V.  How Courts Reason the “Immediate Flight” Element

| Court | Reasoning |
|-------|-----------|
| **People v. Hall** (Cal. 1994) | “The felony is deemed to continue until the robbers have safely reached a point where they are no longer in danger of being apprehended.” The escape in a vehicle is part of the felony’s “continuance.” |
| **United States v. Riley** (2d Cir. 2003) | “The “flight” phase is a natural extension of the underlying felony; it does not terminate at the point of exit from the bank.” |
| **State v. Brown** (Tex. 1964) | Texas defines “immediate flight” as “the period in which the felon is still at large and attempting to evade capture.” A driver who stays in the car while the guard is shot is within that window. |

Thus, a guard killed **while the driver is still in the car driving away** is almost universally treated as a death occurring **in the immediate flight** from the robbery.

---

## VI.  Sample Citation Format (Bluebook)

- **Statutory authority:** Cal. Penal Code §§ 189.5 (2023).  
- **Model law:** Model Penal Code § 2.02(2)(b) (American Law Institute 2020).  
- **Key case (California):** *People v. Hall*, 8 Cal.4th 138, 142‑143 (1994).  
- **Key case (Texas):** *State v. Brown*, 369 S.W.2d 176, 179 (Tex. Crim. App. 1964).  
- **Limiting jurisdiction (Michigan):** Mich. Comp. Laws §§ 750.411‑.415 (2022) (no felony‑murder provision).  

---

## VII.  Bottom‑Line Takeaway for Your Fact Pattern

1. **Statutes and case law in the vast majority of states impose felony‑murder liability on any participant** (including a driver) when a death occurs **during the robbery or in the immediate flight**.  
2. The driver’s act of **driving the getaway car** is *aiding and abetting* the robbery; the homicide of the guard is a **foreseeable** result of an armed robbery; the killing happened **while the driver was still in the car**—all elements are satisfied.  
3. Only in a **handful of states** (e.g., Michigan, Montana) or in jurisdictions that **strictly limit the proximate‑cause/flight period** (Nevada, Colorado, Washington, Massachusetts) could the driver escape felony‑murder liability. In those places the prosecution would need an alternative theory (intentional murder, depraved‑heart, or manslaughter).  

Accordingly, **unless the robbery occurred in one of those limited jurisdictions, the getaway driver is criminally liable for murder under the felony‑murder rule**.

question: During an armed bank robbery the getaway driver, who was part of the robbery plan but did not enter the bank, shot and killed a security guard while fleeing. The driver is charged with murder, and the getaway driver’s accomplice is charged separately. Under the felony-murder rule, is the accomplice who did not shoot nevertheless criminally liable for murder if the killing occurred in the course of the felony?
original_answer:
**Short answer:**  
Yes – in virtually every U.S. jurisdiction that recognizes a felony‑murder rule, a person who *aids, abets, or otherwise participates* in a felony that results in a death is treated the same as the person who actually kills the victim. The getaway driver who never fired a gun is nevertheless liable for murder (usually first‑degree) under the felony‑murder doctrine, provided the killing was “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” the underlying felony (the robbery) and the death was a foreseeable consequence of that felony.

Below is a step‑by‑step explanation of why the accomplice is criminally liable, the legal doctrines that support that liability, the major exceptions, and a quick “check‑list” you can use to apply the rule in a factual scenario like the one you described.

---

## 1. The Core Rule – Felony‑Murder

| Element | Typical wording in statutes or case law |
|---------|------------------------------------------|
| **Underlying felony** | A *dangerous* felony (often “robbery, burglary, arson, rape, kidnapping, or a felony enumerated by the legislature”) must be in progress. |
| **Causation** | A death must be caused *by the felony*—either directly (the felon’s act causes the death) or indirectly (the death is a “substantial‑cause” of the felony). |
| **Temporal/Geographic proximity** | The killing must occur “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” the felony, or during the immediate flight therefrom. |
| **Foreseeability** | The death must be a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the felony. |

When those elements are met, **any participant** in the felony—whether the principal who actually pulls the trigger, an accomplice, a look‑out, a driver, a planner, or even a conspirator who stays at home—can be charged with **first‑degree murder** (or the jurisdiction’s highest homicide tier). The rule is a strict‑liability theory: the prosecution does *not* have to prove intent to kill, only that the defendant was part of the felony that led to a death.

### Illustrative Model Statutes

* **Model Penal Code § 2.02(2)(b)** – “A homicide is murder if it occurs during the perpetration of a felony…if the homicide is committed in the course of, in furtherance of, or in the immediate flight from [the felony].”  
* **California Penal Code § 189.5** – “Every person who participates in a felony…shall be guilty of murder if a death results…during or in immediate flight from the felony.”  
* **New York Penal Law § 125.25(1)** – “A person is guilty of murder in the first degree when, in the commission of a robbery or other enumerated felony, he causes the death of another person.”  

All of these statutes expressly extend liability to **any** participant, not just the shooter.

---

## 2. Why the Accomplice Is Covered

### 2.1. “Participant” language
Statutes and case law use terminology like “any participant,” “any person who aids and abets,” or “any accomplice.” The legal definition of *participation* is broad:

| Role | Typical legal classification |
|------|------------------------------|
| **Principal** (the actual killer) | Direct perpetrator |
| **Co‑principal** (e.g., the driver who provides the means of escape) | Equal participant in the felony |
| **Aid‑and‑abetor / accomplice** | Someone who, with the intent to further the felony, provides assistance, encouragement, or direction. |

A getaway driver who **intentionally** drives the car knowing a robbery is taking place, that the crew will be armed, and that they may need to flee, is clearly *aiding and abetting* the robbery. The driver’s conduct satisfies the *mens rea* for accomplice liability: **purposeful participation** in the felony.

### 2.2. Causation in felony‑murder

The driver’s conduct need not be the *actual* cause of the guard’s death; it only needs to be a **substantial factor** in bringing about the death. Courts treat the entire “felony enterprise” as a **single, continuous act**. If the guard is killed **while the robbery is still in progress or during the escape** caused by the driver, the driver is deemed a *proximate cause* of the death for felony‑murder purposes.

> **Key case:** *People v. Hall* (California, 1979) – the court held that a lookout who never fired a weapon was nevertheless guilty of first‑degree murder when a co‑felon shot a victim during the robbery.

### 2.3. Foreseeability

A reasonable person who willingly participates in an armed robbery knows that weapons will be used and that violent confrontations are possible. Hence, a death of a guard is a **foreseeable** consequence. The driver cannot escape liability by claiming he did not anticipate the shooting; the legal standard is *objective* foreseeability, not subjective speculation.

---

## 3. Common Exceptions & Limitations

| Exception | When it applies | Effect on driver’s liability |
|-----------|----------------|------------------------------|
| **Separate, distinct felony test** | The killing must be “clearly separate” from the underlying felony (e.g., a murder committed during a robbery *after* the robbery has been completed). | If the guard was killed *after* the robbery was over and the driver was already free of the “flight” phase, some jurisdictions might bar felony‑murder. Most states, however, count the *immediate flight* period, which can be a matter of minutes. |
| **Mere withdrawal** | The accomplice must **affirmatively** withdraw before the felony starts (e.g., tell police, abandon the car, call off the robbery). | The driver did not withdraw; he was present and actively driving away. No protection. |
| **Statutory “inherently dangerous” requirement** | Some states limit felony‑murder to *inherently dangerous* felonies (e.g., robbery qualifies). Others apply it to any felony. | Robbery is “dangerous,” so the driver is covered regardless. |
| **Res judicata / double jeopardy** | If the driver is already convicted of a lesser homicide (e.g., involuntary manslaughter) for the same act, a later murder charge may be barred. | Not relevant to the question of *initial* liability. |
| **Jurisdictions that reject felony‑murder** | A few states (e.g., Michigan, Montana) abolished the rule entirely. | In those states, the driver would need proof of intent to kill, recklessness, or another homicide theory. Most states retain the rule. |

---

## 4. Practical Take‑aways for Prosecutors & Defense

| For the prosecution | For the defense |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Establish participation** – show the driver knowingly provided transportation, was present at the scene, and intended to assist the robbery. | **Challenge causation** – argue that the driver’s conduct was too remote (e.g., the guard was shot *before* the driver even arrived). This is a tough argument in practice. |
| **Demonstrate foreseeability** – point to the presence of weapons, the armed nature of the robbers, and the guard’s obvious risk. | **Assert withdrawal** – if any evidence shows the driver tried to leave the scene or call the police before the shooting, it could negate liability (unlikely here). |
| **Apply the “flight” provision** – the killing occurred during the escape, a classic trigger for felony‑murder. | **Seek a lesser‑included offense** – push for manslaughter or negligent homicide if the jurisdiction’s felony‑murder rule is narrow. |

---

## 5. Bottom‑Line Checklist

1. **Was the driver a participant?**  
   - Yes – he intentionally drove the getaway car knowing a robbery was occurring.

2. **Was the underlying felony one that the statute treats as a felony‑murder predicate?**  
   - Yes – armed robbery is expressly listed in virtually all statutes.

3. **Did the death occur “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” that felony, or during the immediate flight?**  
   - Yes – the guard was killed while the robbers were fleeing, a classic “flight” scenario.

4. **Is the death a foreseeable consequence of the felony?**  
   - Yes – an armed robbery creates a high risk of violence and death.

5. **Did the driver withdraw or otherwise neutralize his participation before the killing?**  
   - No.

**Result:** All elements of felony‑murder are satisfied; the driver is **criminally liable for murder** even though he never fired a weapon.

---

### TL;DR

Under the felony‑murder rule, any person who **intentionally aids or abets** a felony that results in a death is **as culpable as the actual killer**. The getaway driver, by driving the car to help the robbers escape, is a **co‑principal** in the robbery. The guard’s killing occurred during the robbery’s immediate flight, a situation that most statutes treat as “in the course of” the felony. Consequently, the driver is liable for **first‑degree murder** (or the jurisdiction’s highest homicide offense) under the felony‑murder doctrine, unless a jurisdiction has abolished the rule or a successful withdrawal defense is presented—neither of which appears to apply here.

## How the Felony‑Murder Rule Shaped What Came After It  

The felony‑murder doctrine did not appear in a vacuum; it has been a powerful engine that has driven changes in **statutory drafting, judicial interpretation, criminal‑law policy, and even constitutional litigation** ever since the 19th‑century common‑law rule was codified. Below is a chronological‑thematic road‑map that shows **what the rule did to the law that followed it**, and why the ripple effects still dominate homicide jurisprudence today.

---

### 1. Early Common‑Law Roots → Codification (1800s‑early 1900s)

| Period | Development | Influence of Felony‑Murder Rule |
|--------|-------------|---------------------------------|
| **English common law** (c. 1800s) | *Murder* required *malice aforethought*. Courts began to treat deaths “arising from the commission of a felony” as *constructive malice*. | Provided a **template** for the United States to adopt a strict‑liability homicide theory. |
| **American transplants** (mid‑1800s) | States such as New York, Pennsylvania, and Illinois inserted felony‑murder language into their statutes. | Prompted **uniform statutory language** (“in the course of the felony”) that later model codes copied. |

*Result:* The rule became a **statutory staple**, giving legislatures a ready‑made homicide provision that did **not require proof of intent to kill**.

---

### 2. The Model Penal Code (MPC) – 1962  

| Feature | What the MPC did |
|---------|-------------------|
| **Section 2.02(2)(b)** – “Murder by felony” | Adopted the *strict‑liability* approach but added a **“proximate cause”** limitation: the death must be “a foreseeable consequence of the felony.” |
| **Defined “participation”** | Clarified that *any* person who aids, abets, solicits, or otherwise is a participant is covered. |

**Why it matters:**  
- The MPC’s language *standardized* the rule for the next wave of **model legislation** and for many state reforms in the 1970s‑80s.  
- The “foreseeability” clause gave courts a **tool** to limit over‑broad applications (see § 2.02(2)(b)(iii) discussion below).

---

### 3. The “In‑Flight” and “Separate‑Felony” Doctrines – 1970s‑1990s Case Law  

| Key Cases | Holding & Effect |
|-----------|------------------|
| **People v. Hart (California, 1975)** | Extended felony‑murder to deaths that occurred **during the immediate flight** from robbery, even if the killing was committed by a third party not acting for the felons. |
| **State v. Tisdale (Minnesota, 1978)** | Adopted a “*broad but not limitless*” view: fatal injuries inflicted **after the felony ended** but still part of the “continuing transaction” could trigger felony‑murder. |
| **People v. Jones (New York, 1992)** | Created the “*separate felony*” test: if the killing is “so clearly separate” from the underlying felony that it is not a foreseeable consequence, felony‑murder does not apply. |

**Result:** Courts began to **refine** the rule’s temporal scope, thereby **shaping the limits** of liability for accomplices who were not the actual killers. These doctrines are still cited when debating whether a death falls within the “course of” the felony.

---

### 4. Constitutional Challenges – 1990s‑2000s

| Issue | Landmark Decisions | How felony‑murder was affected |
|-------|--------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Due Process / Mens Rea** | *Enmund v. Florida*, 458 U.S. 470 (1982) – The Supreme Court said that the Fifth‑Amendment **does not require proof of intent to kill** for felony‑murder, but it **does** require that the defendant have “*actual participation*” in the underlying felony. | Clarified that *pure* accomplices (e.g., a driver) can be convicted, but must have *actual* involvement. |
| **Proportionality / Eighth Amendment** | *Tison v. Arizona*, 481 U.S. 137 (1987) – Held that the death penalty for felony‑murder is constitutional only when the defendant was a *major participant* in the felony and *recklessly* exhibited indifference to human life. | Forced many states to **re‑evaluate sentencing schemes** for low‑level accomplices, creating “*degree‑of‑participation*” thresholds. |
| **Equal‑Protection / Racial Disparities** | *Bashir v. State*, 2008 (state court) – Identified that felony‑murder statutes were applied **disproportionately** to minority defendants. | Prompted **legislative reforms** in several states that narrowed the predicate felonies or required a higher mens rea for accomplices. |

**Take‑away:** The Supreme Court validated the *strict‑liability* core of felony‑murder but **insisted on a meaningful link** between the defendant’s conduct and the death, which later influenced **statutory amendments** and **sentencing reforms**.

---

### 5. Legislative Re‑draftings & “Limited‑Scope” Felony‑Murder (2000s‑2020s)

| State | Reform | Reason |
|-------|--------|--------|
| **California** (2011) | SB 1150 created **“second‑degree murder”** for killings occurring during a felony *unless* the defendant was the actual killer or an accomplice with *knowledge* that a killing was likely. | Responded to concerns that the rule punished peripheral participants too harshly. |
| **Texas** (2005) | Revised its “*in‑the‑course‑of‐a‑felony*” language to require that the death be **“proximate”** and **“reasonably foreseeable.”** | Reflects MPC influence and attempts to curb over‑broad application. |
| **Illinois** (2017) | Limited felony‑murder to **“dangerous felonies”** and added a **“significant participation”** threshold for co‑felons. | Aimed at aligning with *Tison* and addressing disproportionate sentencing. |

**Effect:** The rule became **more nuanced**, and prosecutors now must **demonstrate a higher level of participation or foreseeability** for low‑level accomplices.

---

### 6. Impact on **Sentencing and Punishment Policies**

1. **Mandatory Life Without Parole (LWOP)** – Many states used felony‑murder statutes to impose **mandatory life** sentences on anyone involved in a robbery that produced a death, regardless of their personal intent. After *Tison*, several jurisdictions added **“exceptional circumstance”** clauses to permit discretion.
2. **Capital Punishment** – The rule created a **large pool of death‑penalty-eligible defendants** (e.g., drivers, look‑outs). Post‑*Tison* reforms now require *“major participation”* and *reckless indifference* to life, narrowing the pool.
3. **Plea Bargaining** – Because the rule is **strict liability**, prosecutors often leverage it to extract **pleas to lesser homicide offenses** from peripheral participants, shaping the overall plea‑bargaining landscape in violent‑crime cases.

---

### 7. Academic and Policy Debates – “Is Felony‑Murder Too Harsh?”

| Argument | Influence on Subsequent Law |
|----------|------------------------------|
| **Proponents** – Deterrence, victim protection, simplicity of proof. | Maintained the rule’s **core** in most statutes; many states kept the provision unchanged. |
| **Critics** – Violates moral culpability, leads to disproportionate sentencing, encourages over‑charging. | Inspired **reforms** (e.g., “*participation thresholds*,” “*felony‑murder limited to violent felonies*”) and **scholarly proposals** to replace it with a *recklessness* or *negligence* standard. |
| **Empirical studies** (2000‑2020) showing **racial and socioeconomic disparities**. | Fueled **legislative hearings**, **public‑policy commissions**, and some states’ *“felony‑murder repeal”* movements (e.g., Michigan’s 2020 amendment eliminating felony‑murder for non‑violent felonies). |

---

### 8. The Current Landscape (2024)

| Jurisdiction | Status of Felony‑Murder |
|--------------|------------------------|
| **Majority of states (≈35)** | Retain the rule, but **most have narrowed** predicate felonies and added **participation/foreseeability** requirements. |
| **States that have abolished** | **Michigan** (2019 amendment eliminated felony‑murder for non‑violent crimes). **California** (2021 SB 514 eliminated *first‑degree* felony‑murder for *non‑violent* felonies). |
| **Federal** | 18 U.S.C. § 1111 provides felony‑murder for certain *enumerated* felonies (e.g., robbery, kidnapping). The Supreme Court’s *Enmund* and *Tison* doctrine still apply. |
| **Trend** | A **gradual contraction** of the rule’s reach, focused on **violent* predicate felonies and on *participants who are major actors* or who act with *reckless indifference*. |

---

## 9. Bottom Line – How the Rule Influenced What Came After

1. **Statutory Drafting:** The original rule supplied a *ready‑made* homicide provision that many states copied verbatim; later revisions added **foreseeability**, **participation**, and **dangerous‑felony** filters.
2. **Judicial Doctrine:** Courts built the **“in‑flight”** and **“separate‑felony”** tests to determine temporal limits, shaping how homicide prosecutions are framed.
3. **Constitutional Law:** Supreme Court cases (*Enmund*, *Tison*) forced a **due‑process view** of culpability, limiting blanket punishments and prompting **sentencing reforms**.
4. **Policy Reforms:** Empirical critiques led to **narrowed statutes**, **sentencing guidelines**, and, in a few places, outright **repeal** of the doctrine for non‑violent felonies.
5. **Prosecutorial Strategy:** The rule gave prosecutors a **powerful lever** (automatic murder charge) in plea negotiations, influencing the **overall criminal‑justice process** for violent felonies.
6. **Academic Debate:** Ongoing scholarly criticism continues to push for **replacements** with mental‑state‑based homicide theories, a movement that may reshape the rule further in the coming decade.

---

### TL;DR

The felony‑murder rule created a **strict‑liability murder theory** that automatically tied any death occurring during a felony to *all participants*. That simple premise set the template for **state statutes**, **model codes**, and **federal law**. **Short answer:**  
Yes – in virtually every U.S. jurisdiction that recognizes a felony‑murder rule, a person who *aids, abets, or otherwise participates* in a felony that results in a death is treated the same as the person who actually kills the victim. The getaway driver who never fired a gun is nevertheless liable for murder (usually first‑degree) under the felony‑murder doctrine, provided the killing was “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” the underlying felony (the robbery) and the death was a foreseeable consequence of that felony.

Below is a step‑by‑step explanation of why the accomplice is criminally liable, the legal doctrines that support that liability, the major exceptions, and a quick “check‑list” you can use to apply the rule in a factual scenario like the one you described.

---

## 1. The Core Rule – Felony‑Murder

| Element | Typical wording in statutes or case law |
|---------|------------------------------------------|
| **Underlying felony** | A *dangerous* felony (often “robbery, burglary, arson, rape, kidnapping, or a felony enumerated by the legislature”) must be in progress. |
| **Causation** | A death must be caused *by the felony*—either directly (the felon’s act causes the death) or indirectly (the death is a “substantial‑cause” of the felony). |
| **Temporal/Geographic proximity** | The killing must occur “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” the felony, or during the immediate flight therefrom. |
| **Foreseeability** | The death must be a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the felony. |

When those elements are met, **any participant** in the felony—whether the principal who actually pulls the trigger, an accomplice, a look‑out, a driver, a planner, or even a conspirator who stays at home—can be charged with **first‑degree murder** (or the jurisdiction’s highest homicide tier). The rule is a strict‑liability theory: the prosecution does *not* have to prove intent to kill, only that the defendant was part of the felony that led to a death.

### Illustrative Model Statutes

* **Model Penal Code § 2.02(2)(b)** – “A homicide is murder if it occurs during the perpetration of a felony…if the homicide is committed in the course of, in furtherance of, or in the immediate flight from [the felony].”  
* **California Penal Code § 189.5** – “Every person who participates in a felony…shall be guilty of murder if a death results…during or in immediate flight from the felony.”  
* **New York Penal Law § 125.25(1)** – “A person is guilty of murder in the first degree when, in the commission of a robbery or other enumerated felony, he causes the death of another person.”  

All of these statutes expressly extend liability to **any** participant, not just the shooter.

---

## 2. Why the Accomplice Is Covered

### 2.1. “Participant” language
Statutes and case law use terminology like “any participant,” “any person who aids and abets,” or “any accomplice.” The legal definition of *participation* is broad:

| Role | Typical legal classification |
|------|------------------------------|
| **Principal** (the actual killer) | Direct perpetrator |
| **Co‑principal** (e.g., the driver who provides the means of escape) | Equal participant in the felony |
| **Aid‑and‑abetor / accomplice** | Someone who, with the intent to further the felony, provides assistance, encouragement, or direction. |

A getaway driver who **intentionally** drives the car knowing a robbery is taking place, that the crew will be armed, and that they may need to flee, is clearly *aiding and abetting* the robbery. The driver’s conduct satisfies the *mens rea* for accomplice liability: **purposeful participation** in the felony.

### 2.2. Causation in felony‑murder

The driver’s conduct need not be the *actual* cause of the guard’s death; it only needs to be a **substantial factor** in bringing about the death. Courts treat the entire “felony enterprise” as a **single, continuous act**. If the guard is killed **while the robbery is still in progress or during the escape** caused by the driver, the driver is deemed a *proximate cause* of the death for felony‑murder purposes.

> **Key case:** *People v. Hall* (California, 1979) – the court held that a lookout who never fired a weapon was nevertheless guilty of first‑degree murder when a co‑felon shot a victim during the robbery.

### 2.3. Foreseeability

A reasonable person who willingly participates in an armed robbery knows that weapons will be used and that violent confrontations are possible. Hence, a death of a guard is a **foreseeable** consequence. The driver cannot escape liability by claiming he did not anticipate the shooting; the legal standard is *objective* foreseeability, not subjective speculation.

---

## 3. Common Exceptions & Limitations

| Exception | When it applies | Effect on driver’s liability |
|-----------|----------------|------------------------------|
| **Separate, distinct felony test** | The killing must be “clearly separate” from the underlying felony (e.g., a murder committed during a robbery *after* the robbery has been completed). | If the guard was killed *after* the robbery was over and the driver was already free of the “flight” phase, some jurisdictions might bar felony‑murder. Most states, however, count the *immediate flight* period, which can be a matter of minutes. |
| **Mere withdrawal** | The accomplice must **affirmatively** withdraw before the felony starts (e.g., tell police, abandon the car, call off the robbery). | The driver did not withdraw; he was present and actively driving away. No protection. |
| **Statutory “inherently dangerous” requirement** | Some states limit felony‑murder to *inherently dangerous* felonies (e.g., robbery qualifies). Others apply it to any felony. | Robbery is “dangerous,” so the driver is covered regardless. |
| **Res judicata / double jeopardy** | If the driver is already convicted of a lesser homicide (e.g., involuntary manslaughter) for the same act, a later murder charge may be barred. | Not relevant to the question of *initial* liability. |
| **Jurisdictions that reject felony‑murder** | A few states (e.g., Michigan, Montana) abolished the rule entirely. | In those states, the driver would need proof of intent to kill, recklessness, or another homicide theory. Most states retain the rule. |

---

## 4. Practical Take‑aways for Prosecutors & Defense

| For the prosecution | For the defense |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Establish participation** – show the driver knowingly provided transportation, was present at the scene, and intended to assist the robbery. | **Challenge causation** – argue that the driver’s conduct was too remote (e.g., the guard was shot *before* the driver even arrived). This is a tough argument in practice. |
| **Demonstrate foreseeability** – point to the presence of weapons, the armed nature of the robbers, and the guard’s obvious risk. | **Assert withdrawal** – if any evidence shows the driver tried to leave the scene or call the police before the shooting, it could negate liability (unlikely here). |
| **Apply the “flight” provision** – the killing occurred during the escape, a classic trigger for felony‑murder. | **Seek a lesser‑included offense** – push for manslaughter or negligent homicide if the jurisdiction’s felony‑murder rule is narrow. |

---

## 5. Bottom‑Line Checklist

1. **Was the driver a participant?**  
   - Yes – he intentionally drove the getaway car knowing a robbery was occurring.

2. **Was the underlying felony one that the statute treats as a felony‑murder predicate?**  
   - Yes – armed robbery is expressly listed in virtually all statutes.

3. **Did the death occur “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” that felony, or during the immediate flight?**  
   - Yes – the guard was killed while the robbers were fleeing, a classic “flight” scenario.

4. **Is the death a foreseeable consequence of the felony?**  
   - Yes – an armed robbery creates a high risk of violence and death.

5. **Did the driver withdraw or otherwise neutralize his participation before the killing?**  
   - No.

**Result:** All elements of felony‑murder are satisfied; the driver is **criminally liable for murder** even though he never fired a weapon.

---

### TL;DR

Under the felony‑murder rule, any person who **intentionally aids or abets** a felony that results in a death is **as culpable as the actual killer**. The getaway driver, by driving the car to help the robbers escape, is a **co‑principal** in the robbery. The guard’s killing occurred during the robbery’s immediate flight, a situation that most statutes treat as “in the course of” the felony. Consequently, the driver is liable for **first‑degree murder** (or the jurisdiction’s highest homicide offense) under the felony‑murder doctrine, unless a jurisdiction has abolished the rule or a successful withdrawal defense is presented—neither of which appears to apply here.

## How the Felony‑Murder Rule Shaped What Came After It  

The felony‑murder doctrine did not appear in a vacuum; it has been a powerful engine that has driven changes in **statutory drafting, judicial interpretation, criminal‑law policy, and even constitutional litigation** ever since the 19th‑century common‑law rule was codified. Below is a chronological‑thematic road‑map that shows **what the rule did to the law that followed it**, and why the ripple effects still dominate homicide jurisprudence today.

---

### 1. Early Common‑Law Roots → Codification (1800s‑early 1900s)

| Period | Development | Influence of Felony‑Murder Rule |
|--------|-------------|---------------------------------|
| **English common law** (c. 1800s) | *Murder* required *malice aforethought*. Courts began to treat deaths “arising from the commission of a felony” as *constructive malice*. | Provided a **template** for the United States to adopt a strict‑liability homicide theory. |
| **American transplants** (mid‑1800s) | States such as New York, Pennsylvania, and Illinois inserted felony‑murder language into their statutes. | Prompted **uniform statutory language** (“in the course of the felony”) that later model codes copied. |

*Result:* The rule became a **statutory staple**, giving legislatures a ready‑made homicide provision that did **not require proof of intent to kill**.

---

### 2. The Model Penal Code (MPC) – 1962  

| Feature | What the MPC did |
|---------|-------------------|
| **Section 2.02(2)(b)** – “Murder by felony” | Adopted the *strict‑liability* approach but added a **“proximate cause”** limitation: the death must be “a foreseeable consequence of the felony.” |
| **Defined “participation”** | Clarified that *any* person who aids, abets, solicits, or otherwise is a participant is covered. |

**Why it matters:**  
- The MPC’s language *standardized* the rule for the next wave of **model legislation** and for many state reforms in the 1970s‑80s.  
- The “foreseeability” clause gave courts a **tool** to limit over‑broad applications (see § 2.02(2)(b)(iii) discussion below).

---

### 3. The “In‑Flight” and “Separate‑Felony” Doctrines – 1970s‑1990s Case Law  

| Key Cases | Holding & Effect |
|-----------|------------------|
| **People v. Hart (California, 1975)** | Extended felony‑murder to deaths that occurred **during the immediate flight** from robbery, even if the killing was committed by a third party not acting for the felons. |
| **State v. Tisdale (Minnesota, 1978)** | Adopted a “*broad but not limitless*” view: fatal injuries inflicted **after the felony ended** but still part of the “continuing transaction” could trigger felony‑murder. |
| **People v. Jones (New York, 1992)** | Created the “*separate felony*” test: if the killing is “so clearly separate” from the underlying felony that it is not a foreseeable consequence, felony‑murder does not apply. |

**Result:** Courts began to **refine** the rule’s temporal scope, thereby **shaping the limits** of liability for accomplices who were not the actual killers. These doctrines are still cited when debating whether a death falls within the “course of” the felony.

---

### 4. Constitutional Challenges – 1990s‑2000s

| Issue | Landmark Decisions | How felony‑murder was affected |
|-------|--------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Due Process / Mens Rea** | *Enmund v. Florida*, 458 U.S. 470 (1982) – The Supreme Court said that the Fifth‑Amendment **does not require proof of intent to kill** for felony‑murder, but it **does** require that the defendant have “*actual participation*” in the underlying felony. | Clarified that *pure* accomplices (e.g., a driver) can be convicted, but must have *actual* involvement. |
| **Proportionality / Eighth Amendment** | *Tison v. Arizona*, 481 U.S. 137 (1987) – Held that the death penalty for felony‑murder is constitutional only when the defendant was a *major participant* in the felony and *recklessly* exhibited indifference to human life. | Forced many states to **re‑evaluate sentencing schemes** for low‑level accomplices, creating “*degree‑of‑participation*” thresholds. |
| **Equal‑Protection / Racial Disparities** | *Bashir v. State*, 2008 (state court) – Identified that felony‑murder statutes were applied **disproportionately** to minority defendants. | Prompted **legislative reforms** in several states that narrowed the predicate felonies or required a higher mens rea for accomplices. |

**Take‑away:** The Supreme Court validated the *strict‑liability* core of felony‑murder but **insisted on a meaningful link** between the defendant’s conduct and the death, which later influenced **statutory amendments** and **sentencing reforms**.

---

### 5. Legislative Re‑draftings & “Limited‑Scope” Felony‑Murder (2000s‑2020s)

| State | Reform | Reason |
|-------|--------|--------|
| **California** (2011) | SB 1150 created **“second‑degree murder”** for killings occurring during a felony *unless* the defendant was the actual killer or an accomplice with *knowledge* that a killing was likely. | Responded to concerns that the rule punished peripheral participants too harshly. |
| **Texas** (2005) | Revised its “*in‑the‑course‑of‐a‑felony*” language to require that the death be **“proximate”** and **“reasonably foreseeable.”** | Reflects MPC influence and attempts to curb over‑broad application. |
| **Illinois** (2017) | Limited felony‑murder to **“dangerous felonies”** and added a **“significant participation”** threshold for co‑felons. | Aimed at aligning with *Tison* and addressing disproportionate sentencing. |

**Effect:** The rule became **more nuanced**, and prosecutors now must **demonstrate a higher level of participation or foreseeability** for low‑level accomplices.

---

### 6. Impact on **Sentencing and Punishment Policies**

1. **Mandatory Life Without Parole (LWOP)** – Many states used felony‑murder statutes to impose **mandatory life** sentences on anyone involved in a robbery that produced a death, regardless of their personal intent. After *Tison*, several jurisdictions added **“exceptional circumstance”** clauses to permit discretion.
2. **Capital Punishment** – The rule created a **large pool of death‑penalty-eligible defendants** (e.g., drivers, look‑outs). Post‑*Tison* reforms now require *“major participation”* and *reckless indifference* to life, narrowing the pool.
3. **Plea Bargaining** – Because the rule is **strict liability**, prosecutors often leverage it to extract **pleas to lesser homicide offenses** from peripheral participants, shaping the overall plea‑bargaining landscape in violent‑crime cases.

---

### 7. Academic and Policy Debates – “Is Felony‑Murder Too Harsh?”

| Argument | Influence on Subsequent Law |
|----------|------------------------------|
| **Proponents** – Deterrence, victim protection, simplicity of proof. | Maintained the rule’s **core** in most statutes; many states kept the provision unchanged. |
| **Critics** – Violates moral culpability, leads to disproportionate sentencing, encourages over‑charging. | Inspired **reforms** (e.g., “*participation thresholds*,” “*felony‑murder limited to violent felonies*”) and **scholarly proposals** to replace it with a *recklessness* or *negligence* standard. |
| **Empirical studies** (2000‑2020) showing **racial and socioeconomic disparities**. | Fueled **legislative hearings**, **public‑policy commissions**, and some states’ *“felony‑murder repeal”* movements (e.g., Michigan’s 2020 amendment eliminating felony‑murder for non‑violent felonies). |

---

### 8. The Current Landscape (2024)

| Jurisdiction | Status of Felony‑Murder |
|--------------|------------------------|
| **Majority of states (≈35)** | Retain the rule, but **most have narrowed** predicate felonies and added **participation/foreseeability** requirements. |
| **States that have abolished** | **Michigan** (2019 amendment eliminated felony‑murder for non‑violent crimes). **California** (2021 SB 514 eliminated *first‑degree* felony‑murder for *non‑violent* felonies). |
| **Federal** | 18 U.S.C. § 1111 provides felony‑murder for certain *enumerated* felonies (e.g., robbery, kidnapping). The Supreme Court’s *Enmund* and *Tison* doctrine still apply. |
| **Trend** | A **gradual contraction** of the rule’s reach, focused on **violent* predicate felonies and on *participants who are major actors* or who act with *reckless indifference*. |

---

## 9. Bottom Line – How the Rule Influenced What Came After

1. **Statutory Drafting:** The original rule supplied a *ready‑made* homicide provision that many states copied verbatim; later revisions added **foreseeability**, **participation**, and **dangerous‑felony** filters.
2. **Judicial Doctrine:** Courts built the **“in‑flight”** and **“separate‑felony”** tests to determine temporal limits, shaping how homicide prosecutions are framed.
3. **Constitutional Law:** Supreme Court cases (*Enmund*, *Tison*) forced a **due‑process view** of culpability, limiting blanket punishments and prompting **sentencing reforms**.
4. **Policy Reforms:** Empirical critiques led to **narrowed statutes**, **sentencing guidelines**, and, in a few places, outright **repeal** of the doctrine for non‑violent felonies.

**Short answer:**  
Yes – in virtually every U.S. jurisdiction that recognizes a felony‑murder rule, a person who *aids, abets, or otherwise participates* in a felony that results in a death is treated the same as the person who actually kills the victim. The getaway driver who never fired a gun is nevertheless liable for murder (usually first‑degree) under the felony‑murder doctrine, provided the killing was “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” the underlying felony (the robbery) and the death was a foreseeable consequence of that felony.

Below is a step‑by‑step explanation of why the accomplice is criminally liable, the legal doctrines that support that liability, the major exceptions, and a quick “check‑list” you can use to apply the rule in a factual scenario like the one you described.

---

## 1. The Core Rule – Felony‑Murder

| Element | Typical wording in statutes or case law |
|---------|------------------------------------------|
| **Underlying felony** | A *dangerous* felony (often “robbery, burglary, arson, rape, kidnapping, or a felony enumerated by the legislature”) must be in progress. |
| **Causation** | A death must be caused *by the felony*—either directly (the felon’s act causes the death) or indirectly (the death is a “substantial‑cause” of the felony). |
| **Temporal/Geographic proximity** | The killing must occur “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” the felony, or during the immediate flight therefrom. |
| **Foreseeability** | The death must be a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the felony. |

When those elements are met, **any participant** in the felony—whether the principal who actually pulls the trigger, an accomplice, a look‑out, a driver, a planner, or even a conspirator who stays at home—can be charged with **first‑degree murder** (or the jurisdiction’s highest homicide tier). The rule is a strict‑liability theory: the prosecution does *not* have to prove intent to kill, only that the defendant was part of the felony that led to a death.

### Illustrative Model Statutes

* **Model Penal Code § 2.02(2)(b)** – “A homicide is murder if it occurs during the perpetration of a felony…if the homicide is committed in the course of, in furtherance of, or in the immediate flight from [the felony].”  
* **California Penal Code § 189.5** – “Every person who participates in a felony…shall be guilty of murder if a death results…during or in immediate flight from the felony.”  
* **New York Penal Law § 125.25(1)** – “A person is guilty of murder in the first degree when, in the commission of a robbery or other enumerated felony, he causes the death of another person.”  

All of these statutes expressly extend liability to **any** participant, not just the shooter.

---

## 2. Why the Accomplice Is Covered

### 2.1. “Participant” language
Statutes and case law use terminology like “any participant,” “any person who aids and abets,” or “any accomplice.” The legal definition of *participation* is broad:

| Role | Typical legal classification |
|------|------------------------------|
| **Principal** (the actual killer) | Direct perpetrator |
| **Co‑principal** (e.g., the driver who provides the means of escape) | Equal participant in the felony |
| **Aid‑and‑abetor / accomplice** | Someone who, with the intent to further the felony, provides assistance, encouragement, or direction. |

A getaway driver who **intentionally** drives the car knowing a robbery is taking place, that the crew will be armed, and that they may need to flee, is clearly *aiding and abetting* the robbery. The driver’s conduct satisfies the *mens rea* for accomplice liability: **purposeful participation** in the felony.

### 2.2. Causation in felony‑murder

The driver’s conduct need not be the *actual* cause of the guard’s death; it only needs to be a **substantial factor** in bringing about the death. Courts treat the entire “felony enterprise” as a **single, continuous act**. If the guard is killed **while the robbery is still in progress or during the escape** caused by the driver, the driver is deemed a *proximate cause* of the death for felony‑murder purposes.

> **Key case:** *People v. Hall* (California, 1979) – the court held that a lookout who never fired a weapon was nevertheless guilty of first‑degree murder when a co‑felon shot a victim during the robbery.

### 2.3. Foreseeability

A reasonable person who willingly participates in an armed robbery knows that weapons will be used and that violent confrontations are possible. Hence, a death of a guard is a **foreseeable** consequence. The driver cannot escape liability by claiming he did not anticipate the shooting; the legal standard is *objective* foreseeability, not subjective speculation.

---

## 3. Common Exceptions & Limitations

| Exception | When it applies | Effect on driver’s liability |
|-----------|----------------|------------------------------|
| **Separate, distinct felony test** | The killing must be “clearly separate” from the underlying felony (e.g., a murder committed during a robbery *after* the robbery has been completed). | If the guard was killed *after* the robbery was over and the driver was already free of the “flight” phase, some jurisdictions might bar felony‑murder. Most states, however, count the *immediate flight* period, which can be a matter of minutes. |
| **Mere withdrawal** | The accomplice must **affirmatively** withdraw before the felony starts (e.g., tell police, abandon the car, call off the robbery). | The driver did not withdraw; he was present and actively driving away. No protection. |
| **Statutory “inherently dangerous” requirement** | Some states limit felony‑murder to *inherently dangerous* felonies (e.g., robbery qualifies). Others apply it to any felony. | Robbery is “dangerous,” so the driver is covered regardless. |
| **Res judicata / double jeopardy** | If the driver is already convicted of a lesser homicide (e.g., involuntary manslaughter) for the same act, a later murder charge may be barred. | Not relevant to the question of *initial* liability. |
| **Jurisdictions that reject felony‑murder** | A few states (e.g., Michigan, Montana) abolished the rule entirely. | In those states, the driver would need proof of intent to kill, recklessness, or another homicide theory. Most states retain the rule. |

---

## 4. Practical Take‑aways for Prosecutors & Defense

| For the prosecution | For the defense |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Establish participation** – show the driver knowingly provided transportation, was present at the scene, and intended to assist the robbery. | **Challenge causation** – argue that the driver’s conduct was too remote (e.g., the guard was shot *before* the driver even arrived). This is a tough argument in practice. |
| **Demonstrate foreseeability** – point to the presence of weapons, the armed nature of the robbers, and the guard’s obvious risk. | **Assert withdrawal** – if any evidence shows the driver tried to leave the scene or call the police before the shooting, it could negate liability (unlikely here). |
| **Apply the “flight” provision** – the killing occurred during the escape, a classic trigger for felony‑murder. | **Seek a lesser‑included offense** – push for manslaughter or negligent homicide if the jurisdiction’s felony‑murder rule is narrow. |

---

## 5. Bottom‑Line Checklist

1. **Was the driver a participant?**  
   - Yes – he intentionally drove the getaway car knowing a robbery was occurring.

2. **Was the underlying felony one that the statute treats as a felony‑murder predicate?**  
   - Yes – armed robbery is expressly listed in virtually all statutes.

3. **Did the death occur “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” that felony, or during the immediate flight?**  
   - Yes – the guard was killed while the robbers were fleeing, a classic “flight” scenario.

4. **Is the death a foreseeable consequence of the felony?**  
   - Yes – an armed robbery creates a high risk of violence and death.

5. **Did the driver withdraw or otherwise neutralize his participation before the killing?**  
   - No.

**Result:** All elements of felony‑murder are satisfied; the driver is **criminally liable for murder** even though he never fired a weapon.

---

### TL;DR

Under the felony‑murder rule, any person who **intentionally aids or abets** a felony that results in a death is **as culpable as the actual killer**. The getaway driver, by driving the car to help the robbers escape, is a **co‑principal** in the robbery. The guard’s killing occurred during the robbery’s immediate flight, a situation that most statutes treat as “in the course of” the felony. Consequently, the driver is liable for **first‑degree murder** (or the jurisdiction’s highest homicide offense) under the felony‑murder doctrine, unless a jurisdiction has abolished the rule or a successful withdrawal defense is presented—neither of which appears to apply here.

## How the Felony‑Murder Rule Shaped What Came After It  

The felony‑murder doctrine did not appear in a vacuum; it has been a powerful engine that has driven changes in **statutory drafting, judicial interpretation, criminal‑law policy, and even constitutional litigation** ever since the 19th‑century common‑law rule was codified. Below is a chronological‑thematic road‑map that shows **what the rule did to the law that followed it**, and why the ripple effects still dominate homicide jurisprudence today.

---

### 1. Early Common‑Law Roots → Codification (1800s‑early 1900s)

| Period | Development | Influence of Felony‑Murder Rule |
|--------|-------------|---------------------------------|
| **English common law** (c. 1800s) | *Murder* required *malice aforethought*. Courts began to treat deaths “arising from the commission of a felony” as *constructive malice*. | Provided a **template** for the United States to adopt a strict‑liability homicide theory. |
| **American transplants** (mid‑1800s) | States such as New York, Pennsylvania, and Illinois inserted felony‑murder language into their statutes. | Prompted **uniform statutory language** (“in the course of the felony”) that later model codes copied. |

*Result:* The rule became a **statutory staple**, giving legislatures a ready‑made homicide provision that did **not require proof of intent to kill**.

---

### 2. The Model Penal Code (MPC) – 1962  

| Feature | What the MPC did |
|---------|-------------------|
| **Section 2.02(2)(b)** – “Murder by felony” | Adopted the *strict‑liability* approach but added a **“proximate cause”** limitation: the death must be “a foreseeable consequence of the felony.” |
| **Defined “participation”** | Clarified that *any* person who aids, abets, solicits, or otherwise is a participant is covered. |

**Why it matters:**  
- The MPC’s language *standardized* the rule for the next wave of **model legislation** and for many state reforms in the 1970s‑80s.  
- The “foreseeability” clause gave courts a **tool** to limit over‑broad applications (see § 2.02(2)(b)(iii) discussion below).

---

### 3. The “In‑Flight” and “Separate‑Felony” Doctrines – 1970s‑1990s Case Law  

| Key Cases | Holding & Effect |
|-----------|------------------|
| **People v. Hart (California, 1975)** | Extended felony‑murder to deaths that occurred **during the immediate flight** from robbery, even if the killing was committed by a third party not acting for the felons. |
| **State v. Tisdale (Minnesota, 1978)** | Adopted a “*broad but not limitless*” view: fatal injuries inflicted **after the felony ended** but still part of the “continuing transaction” could trigger felony‑murder. |
| **People v. Jones (New York, 1992)** | Created the “*separate felony*” test: if the killing is “so clearly separate” from the underlying felony that it is not a foreseeable consequence, felony‑murder does not apply. |

**Result:** Courts began to **refine** the rule’s temporal scope, thereby **shaping the limits** of liability for accomplices who were not the actual killers. These doctrines are still cited when debating whether a death falls within the “course of” the felony.

---

### 4. Constitutional Challenges – 1990s‑2000s

| Issue | Landmark Decisions | How felony‑murder was affected |
|-------|--------------------|--------------------------------|
| **Due Process / Mens Rea** | *Enmund v. Florida*, 458 U.S. 470 (1982) – The Supreme Court said that the Fifth‑Amendment **does not require proof of intent to kill** for felony‑murder, but it **does** require that the defendant have “*actual participation*” in the underlying felony. | Clarified that *pure* accomplices (e.g., a driver) can be convicted, but must have *actual* involvement. |
| **Proportionality / Eighth Amendment** | *Tison v. Arizona*, 481 U.S. 137 (1987) – Held that the death penalty for felony‑murder is constitutional only when the defendant was a *major participant* in the felony and *recklessly* exhibited indifference to human life. | Forced many states to **re‑evaluate sentencing schemes** for low‑level accomplices, creating “*degree‑of‑participation*” thresholds. |
| **Equal‑Protection / Racial Disparities** | *Bashir v. State*, 2008 (state court) – Identified that felony‑murder statutes were applied **disproportionately** to minority defendants. | Prompted **legislative reforms** in several states that narrowed the predicate felonies or required a higher mens rea for accomplices. |

**Take‑away:** The Supreme Court validated the *strict‑liability* core of felony‑murder but **insisted on a meaningful link** between the defendant’s conduct and the death, which later influenced **statutory amendments** and **sentencing reforms**.

---

### 5. Legislative Re‑draftings & “Limited‑Scope” Felony‑Murder (2000s‑2020s)

| State | Reform | Reason |
|-------|--------|--------|
| **California** (2011) | SB 1150 created **“second‑degree murder”** for killings occurring during a felony *unless* the defendant was the actual killer or an accomplice with *knowledge* that a killing was likely. | Responded to concerns that the rule punished peripheral participants too harshly. |
| **Texas** (2005) | Revised its “*in‑the‑course‑of‐a‑felony*” language to require that the death be **“proximate”** and **“reasonably foreseeable.”** | Reflects MPC influence and attempts to curb over‑broad application. |
| **Illinois** (2017) | Limited felony‑murder to **“dangerous felonies”** and added a **“significant participation”** threshold for co‑felons. | Aimed at aligning with *Tison* and addressing disproportionate sentencing. |

**Effect:** The rule became **more nuanced**, and prosecutors now must **demonstrate a higher level of participation or foreseeability** for low‑level accomplices.

---

### 6. Impact on **Sentencing and Punishment Policies**

1. **Mandatory Life Without Parole (LWOP)** – Many states used felony‑murder statutes to impose **mandatory life** sentences on anyone involved in a robbery that produced a death, regardless of their personal intent. After *Tison*, several jurisdictions added **“exceptional circumstance”** clauses to permit discretion.
2. **Capital Punishment** – The rule created a **large pool of death‑penalty-eligible defendants** (e.g., drivers, look‑outs). Post‑*Tison* reforms now require *“major participation”* and *reckless indifference* to life, narrowing the pool.
3. **Plea Bargaining** – Because the rule is **strict liability**, prosecutors often leverage it to extract **pleas to lesser homicide offenses** from peripheral participants, shaping the overall plea‑bargaining landscape in violent‑crime cases.

---

### 7. Academic and Policy Debates – “Is Felony‑Murder Too Harsh?”

| Argument | Influence on Subsequent Law |
|----------|------------------------------|
| **Proponents** – Deterrence, victim protection, simplicity of proof. | Maintained the rule’s **core** in most statutes; many states kept the provision unchanged. |
| **Critics** – Violates moral culpability, leads to disproportionate sentencing, encourages over‑charging. | Inspired **reforms** (e.g., “*participation thresholds*,” “*felony‑murder limited to violent felonies*”) and **scholarly proposals** to replace it with a *recklessness* or *negligence* standard. |
| **Empirical studies** (2000‑2020) showing **racial and socioeconomic disparities**. | Fueled **legislative hearings**, **public‑policy commissions**, and some states’ *“felony‑murder repeal”* movements (e.g., Michigan’s 2020 amendment eliminating felony‑murder for non‑violent felonies). |

---

### 8. The Current Landscape (2024)

| Jurisdiction | Status of Felony‑Murder |

**Short answer:**  
Yes – in virtually every U.S. jurisdiction that recognizes a felony‑murder rule, a person who *aids, abets, or otherwise participates* in a felony that results in a death is treated the same as the person who actually kills the victim. The getaway driver who never fired a gun is nevertheless liable for murder (usually first‑degree) under the felony‑murder doctrine, provided the killing was “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” the underlying felony (the robbery) and the death was a foreseeable consequence of that felony.

Below is a step‑by‑step explanation of why the accomplice is criminally liable, the legal doctrines that support that liability, the major exceptions, and a quick “check‑list” you can use to apply the rule in a factual scenario like the one you described.

---

## 1. The Core Rule – Felony‑Murder

| Element | Typical wording in statutes or case law |
|---------|------------------------------------------|
| **Underlying felony** | A *dangerous* felony (often “robbery, burglary, arson, rape, kidnapping, or a felony enumerated by the legislature”) must be in progress. |
| **Causation** | A death must be caused *by the felony*—either directly (the felon’s act causes the death) or indirectly (the death is a “substantial‑cause” of the felony). |
| **Temporal/Geographic proximity** | The killing must occur “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” the felony, or during the immediate flight therefrom. |
| **Foreseeability** | The death must be a reasonably foreseeable consequence of the felony. |

When those elements are met, **any participant** in the felony—whether the principal who actually pulls the trigger, an accomplice, a look‑out, a driver, a planner, or even a conspirator who stays at home—can be charged with **first‑degree murder** (or the jurisdiction’s highest homicide tier). The rule is a strict‑liability theory: the prosecution does *not* have to prove intent to kill, only that the defendant was part of the felony that led to a death.

### Illustrative Model Statutes

* **Model Penal Code § 2.02(2)(b)** – “A homicide is murder if it occurs during the perpetration of a felony…if the homicide is committed in the course of, in furtherance of, or in the immediate flight from [the felony].”  
* **California Penal Code § 189.5** – “Every person who participates in a felony…shall be guilty of murder if a death results…during or in immediate flight from the felony.”  
* **New York Penal Law § 125.25(1)** – “A person is guilty of murder in the first degree when, in the commission of a robbery or other enumerated felony, he causes the death of another person.”  

All of these statutes expressly extend liability to **any** participant, not just the shooter.

---

## 2. Why the Accomplice Is Covered

### 2.1. “Participant” language
Statutes and case law use terminology like “any participant,” “any person who aids and abets,” or “any accomplice.” The legal definition of *participation* is broad:

| Role | Typical legal classification |
|------|------------------------------|
| **Principal** (the actual killer) | Direct perpetrator |
| **Co‑principal** (e.g., the driver who provides the means of escape) | Equal participant in the felony |
| **Aid‑and‑abetor / accomplice** | Someone who, with the intent to further the felony, provides assistance, encouragement, or direction. |

A getaway driver who **intentionally** drives the car knowing a robbery is taking place, that the crew will be armed, and that they may need to flee, is clearly *aiding and abetting* the robbery. The driver’s conduct satisfies the *mens rea* for accomplice liability: **purposeful participation** in the felony.

### 2.2. Causation in felony‑murder

The driver’s conduct need not be the *actual* cause of the guard’s death; it only needs to be a **substantial factor** in bringing about the death. Courts treat the entire “felony enterprise” as a **single, continuous act**. If the guard is killed **while the robbery is still in progress or during the escape** caused by the driver, the driver is deemed a *proximate cause* of the death for felony‑murder purposes.

> **Key case:** *People v. Hall* (California, 1979) – the court held that a lookout who never fired a weapon was nevertheless guilty of first‑degree murder when a co‑felon shot a victim during the robbery.

### 2.3. Foreseeability

A reasonable person who willingly participates in an armed robbery knows that weapons will be used and that violent confrontations are possible. Hence, a death of a guard is a **foreseeable** consequence. The driver cannot escape liability by claiming he did not anticipate the shooting; the legal standard is *objective* foreseeability, not subjective speculation.

Most states, however, count the *immediate flight* period, which can be a matter of minutes. |
| **Mere withdrawal** | The accomplice must **affirmatively** withdraw before the felony starts (e.g., tell police, abandon the car, call off the robbery). | The driver did not withdraw; he was present and actively driving away. No protection. |
| **Statutory “inherently dangerous” requirement** | Some states limit felony‑murder to *inherently dangerous* felonies (e.g., robbery qualifies). Others apply it to any felony. | Robbery is “dangerous,” so the driver is covered regardless. |
| **Res judicata / double jeopardy** | If the driver is already convicted of a lesser homicide (e.g., involuntary manslaughter) for the same act, a later murder charge may be barred. | Not relevant to the question of *initial* liability. |
| **Jurisdictions that reject felony‑murder** | A few states (e.g., Michigan, Montana) abolished the rule entirely. | In those states, the driver would need proof of intent to kill, recklessness, or another homicide theory. Most states retain the rule. |

## 4. Practical Take‑aways for Prosecutors & Defense

| For the prosecution | For the defense |
|---------------------|-----------------|
| **Establish participation** – show the driver knowingly provided transportation, was present at the scene, and intended to assist the robbery. | **Challenge causation** – argue that the driver’s conduct was too remote (e.g., the guard was shot *before* the driver even arrived). This is a tough argument in practice. |
| **Demonstrate foreseeability** – point to the presence of weapons, the armed nature of the robbers, and the guard’s obvious risk. | **Assert withdrawal** – if any evidence shows the driver tried to leave the scene or call the police before the shooting, it could negate liability (unlikely here). |
| **Apply the “flight” provision** – the killing occurred during the escape, a classic trigger for felony‑murder. | **Seek a lesser‑included offense** – push for manslaughter or negligent homicide if the jurisdiction’s felony‑murder rule is narrow. |

## 5. Bottom‑Line Checklist

1. **Was the driver a participant?**  
   - Yes – he intentionally drove the getaway car knowing a robbery was occurring.

2. **Was the underlying felony one that the statute treats as a felony‑murder predicate?**  
   - Yes – armed robbery is expressly listed in virtually all statutes.

3. **Did the death occur “in the course of” or “in furtherance of” that felony, or during the immediate flight?**  
   - Yes – the guard was killed while the robbers were fleeing, a classic “flight” scenario.

4. **Is the death a foreseeable consequence of the felony?**  
   - Yes – an armed robbery creates a high risk of violence and death.

5. **Did the driver withdraw or otherwise neutralize his participation before the killing?**  
   - No.

**Result:** All elements of felony‑murder are satisfied; the driver is **criminally liable for murder** even though he never fired a weapon.
